meal_split_full.title: Don't Skip Breakfast
meal_split_full.desc: Breakfast activates metabolism and stabilizes blood sugar throughout the day.
meal_split_full.keyFact: Consistently skipping breakfast raises morning cortisol, slows metabolism, and intensifies sugar/fat cravings at lunch and dinner.
meal_split_full.detail: Breakfast breaks the overnight fast (8–10 hours), activates thermogenesis (the calorie-burning process of digestion), and stabilizes blood sugar before the brain starts working. No need for a large breakfast — 300–400 kcal with protein + slow carbs is enough.
details: Cortisol naturally peaks in the morning (Cortisol Awakening Response). Skipping breakfast keeps cortisol elevated longer, pushing the body to burn muscle protein instead of fat.
Low morning blood sugar → poor brain function → difficulty concentrating, irritability, increased cravings for sweets as a quick fix.
Ideal breakfast: 300–400 kcal, 20–30g protein, slow carbs (oatmeal, whole-grain bread) — no need for perfect macros.
No time? Boiled eggs + milk + banana = 5 minutes, 350 kcal, 25g protein. Enough to kick-start the day.
If you genuinely can't eat in the morning (no appetite), eat within 1 hour of waking instead of skipping entirely.

points.note: Burn calories from the first meal

meal_split_full.title: Protein at Every Meal
meal_split_full.desc: Protein keeps you full longer, protects muscle, and burns extra calories during digestion.
meal_split_full.keyFact: Protein has a TEF (Thermic Effect of Food) of 20–30% — the body burns 20–30 kcal just to digest 100 kcal of protein. Carbs and fat only burn 5–8%.
meal_split_full.detail: Protein is the only macro that simultaneously keeps you full longer (increases PYY, GLP-1, reduces ghrelin), protects muscle during calorie cuts, and generates heat during digestion. Distributing protein evenly across 3–4 meals optimizes muscle protein synthesis (MPS) better than concentrating it in 1–2 meals.
details: Protein target: 1.6–2.2g/kg body weight/day. Split evenly across 3–4 meals, 25–40g each — optimal for muscle protein synthesis (MPS).
Complete protein sources (all 9 essential amino acids): meat, fish, eggs, dairy, soy. Combining rice + beans also creates complete protein.
Protein slows the overall digestion rate of a meal, stabilizing post-meal blood sugar — better effect if eating protein BEFORE carbs in the same meal.
Protein snacks (yogurt, cheese sticks, boiled eggs) control between-meal hunger better than pure-carb snacks like crackers.
Strength trainers need 2.0–2.2g/kg; those maintaining or losing slightly need 1.6–1.8g/kg; sedentary individuals need at least 1.2g/kg.

meal_split_full.title: Eat Vegetables Before Carbs
meal_split_full.desc: Vegetables slow sugar absorption and reduce the insulin spike after meals.
meal_split_full.keyFact: Eating vegetables before rice can reduce the post-meal blood sugar peak by 40–50% compared to eating rice first — Weill Cornell Medicine research.
meal_split_full.detail: Fiber in vegetables creates a viscous gel layer in the intestine, slowing amylase enzymes that break down starch and reducing glucose absorption into the blood. Result: lower insulin peak, longer fullness, and less fat storage even eating the same calories.
details: Mechanism: soluble fiber (pectin, beta-glucan) forms a gel coating the small intestine wall, slowing starch-digesting enzymes and glucose absorption.
Weill Cornell study (2015): eating veg/protein before rice reduced glucose peak by 37–40% vs. eating rice first. Effect lasts up to 2 hours after the meal.
No need to eat each item separately — just start the meal with a few bites of vegetable before eating rice to create the buffering effect.
Most effective vegetables: broccoli, cauliflower, leafy greens, okra (high soluble fiber). At least 1–2 handfuls of veg per main meal.
Similar effect occurs with protein — eating protein before carbs also slows glucose absorption. Combining veg + protein before rice is the optimal strategy.

points.label: 40% glucose reduction
points.note: Stabilizes blood sugar after meals

points.note: Creates gel, slows carb absorption

points.note: Just a few bites first is enough

meal_split_full.title: Proper Meal Spacing
meal_split_full.desc: Don't go more than 5 hours without eating — prevents overeating at the next meal.
meal_split_full.keyFact: Ideal meal spacing: 3–5 hours. Under 3 hours: insulin hasn't returned to baseline. Over 5 hours: blood sugar too low → uncontrolled eating binge.
meal_split_full.detail: Meal spacing affects hunger/satiety hormones (ghrelin/leptin), blood sugar levels, and eating psychology. Going too long without food triggers 'emergency eating' — the brain prioritizes high-calorie foods, eats fast, and barely registers fullness until well past overeating.
details: Ghrelin (hunger hormone) peaks after 4–5 hours without food. When ghrelin is too high, portion control drops significantly — the brain prioritizes high-energy, fast foods.
3–5 hour spacing: optimal for fully digesting the previous meal, allowing insulin to return to baseline before starting a new meal.
A 100–200 kcal snack after 3–4 hours (when meals are far apart) helps prevent ghrelin from peaking too high and keeps energy stable.
No need to eat at exactly the same time every day — what matters is TOTAL calories and spacing enough to avoid being too hungry before main meals.
Signs of poor meal spacing: eating very fast, not feeling full even after eating a lot, intense sweet/salty cravings after meals.

meal_split_full.title: Light Dinner
meal_split_full.desc: Reduce starchy carbs at dinner if not training; increase vegetables and protein instead.
meal_split_full.keyFact: Insulin sensitivity decreases 20–25% in the evening compared to the morning — the same amount of carbs at dinner will raise blood sugar higher and store fat more easily than at breakfast.
meal_split_full.detail: The body has a circadian rhythm that affects how different foods are processed. Evening: insulin less sensitive, metabolism slower, body preparing for sleep. A heavy, carb-rich dinner raises blood sugar and reduces sleep quality.
details: Circadian rhythm and insulin: insulin receptors work best in the morning, less responsive in the evening. Eating many carbs at night = same carbs but higher blood sugar than in the morning.
Ideal dinner: moderate protein (30–40g) + lots of vegetables (fiber helps fullness, stabilizes evening blood sugar) + minimal carbs (small sweet potato or brown rice).
Exception: if you train in the evening, the body needs carbs after training to replenish glycogen. Eating carbs after a late workout is necessary — not wrong.
Eating dinner too full or too close to bedtime (less than 2 hours) reduces sleep quality: higher body temperature, digestion competes with overnight recovery.
Simple dinner: steamed fish/chicken + vegetable soup + small portion of brown rice. 400–500 kcal total, filling, easy to digest, doesn't disrupt sleep.

tdee_benefits_full.title: Eat on Target
tdee_benefits_full.desc: Know exactly how many kcal you need per day — no guessing when you want to lose fat, gain muscle, or maintain.
tdee_benefits_full.keyFact: A ±200 kcal/day deviation from your actual TDEE can make or break a fat loss/muscle gain journey in just 2–3 weeks.
tdee_benefits_full.detail: Without knowing your TDEE, you're guessing your daily calories. On average, people underestimate their food intake by 20–40%. TDEE gives you a concrete number to adjust toward your exact goal — fat loss (cut 400 kcal), maintenance (match TDEE), or muscle gain (add 300 kcal).
details: Fat loss goal: eat TDEE − 400 kcal/day. This is a safe deficit that doesn't burn muscle or lower your BMR (basal metabolic rate).
Muscle gain goal: eat TDEE + 300 kcal/day. A modest surplus helps build muscle without accumulating too much fat.
Maintenance goal: eat exactly TDEE. This is the most stable body state — no loss, no gain.
Many people fail not from lack of willpower, but from not knowing how much they're eating. TDEE provides a concrete 'anchor' to hold to.
No need to count every calorie forever — just track for 2–4 weeks to recalibrate your brain's sense of hunger to actual needs.

tdee_benefits_full.title: Avoid Energy Imbalance
tdee_benefits_full.desc: Eat enough to maintain energy and muscle, avoid 'crash' from aggressive cuts or fat gain from overeating.
tdee_benefits_full.keyFact: Cutting calories below BMR (resting energy) triggers 'starvation mode' — the body burns muscle instead of fat and reduces BMR by up to 20%.
tdee_benefits_full.detail: Chronic energy deficiency (eating below BMR) causes metabolic adaptation: the body lowers its BMR to survive, burns muscle for fuel, and stores fat again as soon as normal eating resumes. Conversely, large caloric surplus (>500 kcal/day) stores fat faster than it builds muscle.
details: BMR (Basal Metabolic Rate) is the minimum energy for organs to function at complete rest. Eating below BMR = the body 'eating' itself.
'Metabolic adaptation' after aggressive calorie cuts: BMR drops 10–20%, body prioritizes burning muscle protein over stored fat.
Signs of chronic energy deficiency: afternoon fatigue, difficulty concentrating, intense sugar cravings, poor sleep quality, hair loss.
Large surplus (>500 kcal/day) doesn't build muscle faster — it only accelerates fat storage, worsening the muscle-to-fat ratio.
Ideal goal: always stay within −400 to +300 kcal of TDEE. This is the safe 'anabolic window'.

tdee_benefits_full.desc: No progress after 2 weeks? Increase/decrease exactly 100–200 kcal instead of overhauling the entire diet.
tdee_benefits_full.keyFact: Changing 100 kcal/day = 700 kcal/week = ~0.1 kg of fat/week. Small adjustments, clear results, no need to overhaul everything.
tdee_benefits_full.detail: The body adapts to calorie intake after 2–3 weeks. When the scale doesn't move despite your efforts, that's a signal to adjust — not quit. TDEE allows precise fine-tuning instead of trial and error.
details: Plateau is normal — not failure. The body automatically adjusts its TDEE when body weight changes.
No progress after 2 weeks of consistent eating → reduce by another 100–150 kcal/day. Simple, no need to overhaul everything.
No weight gain after 2 weeks of muscle-building training → add 100–150 kcal/day, prioritize protein and carbs around workouts.
Weigh in the morning, after using the bathroom, before eating — take a 7-day average. Daily fluctuations of 0.5–2 kg are normal due to water.
Re-feed day (increasing calories 1 day/week) helps reset leptin, reduces fatigue and mental strain during a long fat-loss phase.

tdee_benefits_full.title: Update as Your Body Changes
tdee_benefits_full.desc: TDEE shifts when weight changes. Recalculate every 4 weeks to stay consistently effective.
tdee_benefits_full.keyFact: Losing 5 kg = TDEE decreases ~100 kcal/day. Without updating → forced plateau after 4–6 weeks even when eating correctly.
tdee_benefits_full.detail: TDEE is not a fixed number — it changes with body weight, age, and activity level. Someone who has lost 5 kg needs fewer calories than they did at 5 kg heavier. Not updating TDEE is the most common reason for inevitable plateaus.
details: Every 1 kg lost/gained → TDEE changes by about 20–25 kcal/day. Losing 5 kg = TDEE drops 100–125 kcal/day.
Recalculate TDEE after every 4 weeks or when weight changes by ≥ 2–3 kg. Re-enter your new weight into the B0 calculator.
Activity level also changes over time — from 'sedentary' to 'moderately active' as you get used to a training schedule.
After 3–6 months of training, muscle-to-fat ratio improves → BMR increases slightly (muscle burns more calories than fat at rest).
No complex app needed: recalculate TDEE every 4 weeks using the B0 tool here — takes 2 minutes, saves 4 weeks of guessing.

c0_items.label: Sleep
c0_items.keyFact: 7–9 hours of quality sleep improves training performance by 20–25% and significantly reduces the risk of chronic disease.
c0_items.detail: Sleep is the foundation of everything — muscle recovery, hormone balance, memory, and appetite control. This is the first metric to assess.
details: Record your bedtime and wake time for 7 consecutive days — this is your real baseline, not your intention.
Quality matters more than quantity: 6 hours of deep sleep beats 8 hours of restless sleep. Rate your quality 1–10 each morning.
Consistent sleep timing (variation ≤60 min each day, including weekends) regulates your circadian clock better than any other habit.
Melatonin starts rising 2 hours before you naturally feel sleepy — blue light from screens and heavy food block this process.
Deep sleep occurs mostly in the first half of the night — going to bed after midnight loses more deep sleep than you'd expect.
If you wake up feeling unrefreshed after 7+ hours → this is a signal to adjust your evening habits, not to drink more coffee.

c0_items.label: Energy
c0_items.desc: When you're most alert, when you're most tired
c0_items.keyFact: Your circadian rhythm determines ~60% of your energy level throughout the day — know your own cycle to work with it, not against it.
c0_items.detail: Energy is not willpower — it's physiology. Knowing when your brain is sharpest and when your body needs rest helps you get the most from every hour.
details: Log your energy level every 2–3 hours for 3 days (1–10): this is the only way to discover your true chronotype.
Most people have energy peaks at 9–11 AM and 3–5 PM, with a sharp dip at 1–3 PM after lunch.
When you're sharpest → do deep cognitive work. When you're most tired → schedule meetings, email, routine tasks.
The Ultradian cycle is ~90 minutes: the brain works at high intensity for ~90 minutes and then needs 10–20 minutes of rest.
Caffeine masks adenosine (the sleepiness molecule) rather than creating real energy — overuse disrupts your natural cycle.
Morning sunlight is the strongest 'reset button' for your circadian clock — even 5 minutes outside after waking is enough.

c0_items.label: Daily movement
c0_items.keyFact: 8,000 steps/day reduces early mortality risk by 51% according to a 2021 JAMA study — and you don't need a gym to reach this number.
c0_items.detail: NEAT — movement outside the gym — can account for 15–50% of total daily energy expenditure. This is the 'secret weapon' most people overlook.
details: Count your current steps before setting a goal — many gym-goers still take only 3,000–4,000 steps because they sit all day.
Sitting >8 hours continuously raises cardiovascular disease risk independently of gym exercise — stand up every 45–60 minutes.
Every additional 1,000 steps above your current baseline creates measurable health benefits — no need to jump straight to 10,000.
Light movement after meals (5–10 min walk) reduces post-meal blood glucose by 20–30%, far more effective than sitting still.
Continuous sitting time matters more than total sitting time: 8 hours of sitting with hourly stand-ups beats 4 hours of unbroken sitting.
Practical target: increase by 500–1,000 steps per week until you naturally reach 7,000–8,000 steps/day.

c0_items.label: Recovery
c0_items.keyFact: 40% of sports injuries and chronic pain don't come from overtraining — they come from insufficient recovery and ignoring early warning signs.
c0_items.detail: Recovery is not passive rest — it's a collection of active practices that help the body rebuild, reduce inflammation, and prepare for the next session.
details: Neck, shoulder, and lower back pain after desk work is a signal of weak muscles and poor posture — not something you just have to accept.
Distinguish delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS — dull ache 1–3 days post-workout) from joint/tendon pain (sharp, localized → rest and check it).
5–10 min of mobility daily is more effective than 1 hour of foam rolling per week — consistency beats recovery intensity.
Signs of overtraining: resting heart rate 5–7 bpm above normal, insomnia despite fatigue, performance declining over 2–3 consecutive sessions.
A deload week (reduce training volume 40–50%) every 4–6 weeks enables deep recovery and typically precedes a performance breakthrough.
Cold/heat, massage, and stretching are all tools — none is universally best. Try them and observe your body's response.

c0_items.label: Evening habits
c0_items.keyFact: Blue-light screens after 8 PM delay melatonin secretion by 1–3 hours and reduce sleep quality by ~20%, according to Harvard research.
c0_items.detail: What you do in the 2 hours before bed determines the quality of the 7–8 hours of sleep that follow. This is the easiest intervention window with the greatest impact.
details: Phone, TV, and laptop screens emit blue light that suppresses melatonin — use Night Mode or blue-light-filtering glasses from 8 PM.
Ideally eat dinner before 8 PM — a heavy meal close to bedtime raises core body temperature, disrupts deep sleep, and increases acid reflux risk.
Stressful work after 9 PM activates cortisol — the brain needs at least 60 minutes away from work before sleep to truly wind down.
Keep the bedroom below 20°C — body temperature drops during sleep, and a cool environment makes this process more natural.
Even a short 5-minute evening routine (shower, light reading, brief journaling) signals to the brain: it's nearly time to sleep.
You don't need to do everything at once — pick 1 habit change, maintain it for 2–3 weeks, then add the next one.

c0_score.label: Sleep ≥7h or improving
c0_score.detail: The most important criterion in the Lifestyle Score — getting enough sleep is the foundation for every other health improvement.
c0_score.keyFact: Just one night of less than 6 hours of sleep reduces memory consolidation by 40% and increases cortisol by 37% the next day.
details: The minimum target is 7 hours — not 8. Research shows 7–9 hours is the optimal range for adults.
'Or improving' means if you previously slept 5 hours and now sleep 6, you still earn the points — progress matters more than perfection.
Quality > quantity: 7 hours of unbroken deep sleep beats 9 hours of fragmented sleep.
Chronic sleep deprivation (under 6 hours for multiple consecutive weeks) is linked to higher risk of type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease.
Weekend sleep catch-up does not erase accumulated sleep debt — it partially restores some cognitive function but cannot undo the metabolic damage.
Simplest strategy: fix your wake time first, then gradually adjust your bedtime.

c0_score.detail: Consistency of sleep timing matters more than total sleep hours — the circadian clock needs to be anchored to a regular schedule.
c0_score.keyFact: Varying sleep time by more than 90 minutes between weekdays and weekends has the same negative metabolic impact as crossing 1–2 time zones every week.
details: 'Relatively consistent' means no more than 60 minutes of variation across days — you don't need to be minute-precise.
The circadian rhythm coordinates over 20,000 genes and hundreds of hormones on a 24-hour cycle.
Sleeping 2 hours later on weekends creates 'social jet lag' — reducing insulin sensitivity and increasing cravings.
Strategy: set a 'bedtime alarm' 30 minutes before your target sleep time — cues the brain to start winding down.
Morning light is the strongest anchor for fixing your circadian rhythm.
If you must stay up 1 hour later: keep your normal wake time and your body will self-correct by the following evening.

c0_score.detail: The two most powerful signals to reset your circadian clock each morning — combine them for a synergistic effect.
c0_score.keyFact: Sunlight exposure in the first 30–60 minutes after waking fully suppresses daytime melatonin and raises cortisol along its natural rhythm.
details: Morning natural light activates ipRGC cells in the eyes — sending a direct signal to the brain's central clock (SCN).
Required intensity: 1,000–10,000 lux (outdoor light), versus only 100–500 lux indoors — this is why going outside matters.
Morning movement (5–15 min walk, stretching) raises core body temperature and dopamine — two wakefulness signals more lasting than caffeine.
No sunshine (rain/winter): a 10,000-lux light therapy lamp for 10–20 minutes still works.
Ideal combination: a 10-minute outdoor walk right after waking — light, movement, and fresh air all at once.
Avoid sunglasses in the first 10–15 minutes outside — glasses filter the UV light needed to trigger the circadian reflex.

NEAT isn't just steps: standing up for 2 minutes every hour, taking stairs, standing while on the phone — it all adds up.
'Hitting the goal' doesn't require 10,000 steps every day — personalize: if your baseline is 3,000, a goal of 5,000 is appropriate.
Walking 10–15 minutes after meals reduces post-meal glucose peaks by 30–50% and improves insulin sensitivity.
Step trackers increase average daily steps by 26% according to a meta-analysis — simply measuring creates motivation.
On a sedentary day: 5 minutes of squats, lunges, or calf raises before bed activates muscles and reduces the negative impact.

c0_score.label: No prolonged sitting
c0_score.detail: Sitting continuously for more than 60–90 minutes is independently harmful — it cannot be 'offset' by an hour at the gym afterward.
c0_score.keyFact: 'Sitting is the new smoking' — sitting continuously for >90 minutes raises metabolic disease risk even in regular gym-goers.
details: Prolonged sitting suppresses lipoprotein lipase (LPL) — the fat-burning enzyme. After 60 minutes, LPL drops 90% in activity.
The 60-minute rule: stand up and move for at least 2–3 minutes after every 60 minutes of sitting.
A study of 800,000 people found those who sat the most (>8h/day) had a 73% higher mortality risk.
Simple tools: set a 50-minute timer, use a standing desk, or place a small water glass to force more frequent stand-ups.
Sitting immediately after eating extends the glucose peak and increases fat storage. 10 minutes of standing after eating helps.
A standing desk alone isn't enough if you stand motionless — alternate sitting and standing every 2 hours.

c0_score.detail: Active recovery, mobility, and intentional breathing — three pillars that shift the autonomic nervous system to parasympathetic mode.
c0_score.keyFact: HRV increases by 18% after 10 minutes of intentional breathing compared to passive rest of the same duration.
details: Active recovery: 10 minutes of foam rolling or gentle joint movement — stimulates blood flow without adding physiological stress.
Mobility is not just stretching: it's the ability to actively control the full range of motion. At least 5 minutes of dynamic mobility daily.
Intentional breathing: the 4-7-8 technique (inhale 4s, hold 7s, exhale 8s) activates the parasympathetic nervous system within 3–5 minutes.
Optimal timing: just before sleep (5–10 min) helps transition from alert to drowsy far more effectively than scrolling.
Minimum to earn the point: 10 minutes/day of any combination of the three elements above.
Signs of insufficient recovery: chronically tight muscles, resting heart rate above normal, difficulty falling asleep, unexplained irritability.

c0_score.detail: The two most common disruptors of sleep quality — blue light from screens and caffeine that lingers in your body far longer than you think.
c0_score.keyFact: Caffeine has a 5–7 hour half-life — one coffee at 3 PM still has 50% activity in your blood at 8–10 PM.
details: Caffeine half-life 5–7 hours: if you drink 200 mg caffeine at 2 PM, ~100 mg is still 'active' at 9 PM.
Evening screens: blue light (~480 nm) is the most effective suppressor of melatonin — phones and laptops 'trick' the brain into thinking it's daytime.
Practical screen solutions: enable Night Mode from 6–7 PM, dim brightness to 30–40% after 8 PM, or wear amber glasses after 9 PM.
Caffeine solutions: a hard cut-off at 1–2 PM if you plan to sleep at 10–11 PM.
Deceptive caffeine sources: green tea 30–50 mg, black tea 40–70 mg, dark chocolate 25 mg/30g — often overlooked.
You don't have to go 'zero screen' from 8 PM — reading with warm lighting is far better than scrolling with a bright screen.

c2_morning_5.label: Drink a glass of water
c2_morning_5.detail: The simplest step with immediate impact — your body is dehydrated after 7–9 hours of sleep.
c2_morning_5.keyFact: Losing just 1–2% of body water reduces cognitive performance by 10–15% — and you typically reach this level the moment you wake up.
details: After 7–9 hours without drinking, your body starts the day in a state of mild dehydration.
The brain is ~75% water — even mild dehydration slows neural transmission and reduces focus.
Drink water before coffee: caffeine on an empty stomach while dehydrated spikes cortisol.
200–300 ml of water is ideal — no need to drink a whole liter at once.
Simple habit cue: place a water bottle on your nightstand the evening before.
The 'not quite awake' feeling after waking typically fades faster after drinking water and getting light.

c2_morning_5.label: Open curtains / Natural light
c2_morning_5.detail: Natural light is the most powerful reset button for your circadian clock — more important than any other morning habit.
c2_morning_5.keyFact: Outdoor light (10,000–100,000 lux) is 100–1,000 times stronger than indoor lighting — 5 minutes outside beats leaving lights on all morning.
details: Your eyes contain special light-sensitive cells (ipRGCs) connected directly to the brain's 'master clock' (SCN).
Morning light activates the Cortisol Awakening Response (CAR) — the good cortisol that makes you alert.
Cloudy or rainy days still work — outdoor light is at least 1,000–2,000 lux even without sun.
Opening curtains still helps if you have a large east-facing window — but not as effective as 5 minutes outside.
Don't wear sunglasses in the first 5 minutes — glasses reduce the benefit.
Morning light also boosts serotonin — the precursor of nighttime melatonin. More serotonin = deeper sleep at night.

c2_morning_5.label: Light walk + joint rotations
c2_morning_5.detail: 60 seconds of gentle movement is enough to wake up your circulatory system and lubricate joints after 7–9 hours lying still.
c2_morning_5.keyFact: 60 seconds of gentle morning movement activates circulation and lubricates joints — reducing stiffness and aches through the day.
details: After 7–9 hours of sleep, synovial fluid in the joints is reduced — gentle movement distributes joint fluid and reduces morning stiffness.
Marching in place for 30–60 seconds pumps blood from legs back to the heart and reduces dizziness.
Shoulder rotations: 10–15 circles each direction releases the trapezius and relieves neck tension effectively.
Hip rotations: the hip joint is the largest in the body and often the stiffest after sleep — 10–15 circles each side.
No space needed — everything can be done right beside the bed.
This 1 minute is a 'notification' to your body that a new day has begun.

c2_morning_5.label: 4–6 deep breaths
c2_morning_5.detail: Close the 5-minute routine with intentional breathing — setting your nervous system frequency for the whole day.
c2_morning_5.keyFact: 4–6 slow diaphragmatic breaths activate the parasympathetic nervous system — reaching the ideal 'calm but alert' state.
details: In the morning, the sympathetic nervous system is often elevated due to rising cortisol — slow deep breaths rebalance toward calm focus.
Simplest technique: inhale through your nose for 4 seconds (belly expands), exhale through mouth for 6 seconds. Repeat 4–6 times.
A longer exhale than inhale activates the vagus nerve — slowing heart rate and lowering blood pressure within 60 seconds.
After 4–6 proper breaths, HRV increases measurably — the most important marker of recovery and focused readiness.
While breathing, ask yourself: 'How do I want to feel today?' — activates the prefrontal cortex.
Just 1 minute but the effect lasts: slow morning breathing establishes a neural 'baseline' for the whole day.

Do both at the same time: drink your water while standing at the open door — saves time and creates a habit combo.
Sunshine not required — a cloudy day still works. Outdoor light is at least 1,000–2,000 lux.

c2_energy_tips.detail: Your eyes contain specialized light-sensitive cells (ipRGCs) directly connected to the body's master clock (SCN). Morning light 'locks in' your wake time and triggers a hormone cascade for the entire day.
details: Morning natural light (10,000–100,000 lux) is 100–1,000 times stronger than indoor lighting (~100–500 lux).
Within the first 30–60 minutes after waking, light exposure activates the Cortisol Awakening Response.
5 minutes of morning natural light doesn't require bright sunshine — a cloudy day still works.
Wearing sunglasses when going outside reduces the effect — let your eyes receive direct light.
If you can't go outside, open the curtains fully and sit close to the window for 10–15 minutes.
Morning light also boosts serotonin — the precursor to nighttime melatonin. More serotonin = deeper sleep at night.

points.label: 5 min is enough
points.note: Go outside right after waking

points.label: Cloudy days still work
points.note: Outdoors is always brighter than indoors

points.label: No sunglasses
points.note: Let your eyes receive natural light

points.label: Within the first hour
points.note: Activates good cortisol for the day

c2_energy_tips.label: Water first thing
c2_energy_tips.desc: Drink 200–300 ml of water right after waking. The body loses water during 7–9 hours of sleep.
c2_energy_tips.keyFact: Losing 1–2% of body water is already enough to reduce cognitive performance 10–15% and increase fatigue.
c2_energy_tips.detail: After 7–9 hours without drinking, your body starts the day mildly dehydrated. Drinking water is one of the simplest morning habits with the clearest benefits.
details: The brain is ~75% water — even mild dehydration slows neural transmission and increases morning grogginess.
Drink water before coffee: caffeine on an empty stomach while dehydrated spikes cortisol.
200–300 ml is the ideal amount — no need to drink a full liter; sip slowly over the first 10–15 minutes.
Plain water or warm water are both fine. Adding a pinch of salt or lemon is optional.
Place a water bottle on your nightstand the evening before — removes all friction.
The 'sleepy' feeling in the first 10–20 minutes after waking typically fades faster after drinking water and getting light.

points.label: 200–300 ml right away
points.note: Before coffee and breakfast

points.label: Bottle on the nightstand
points.note: Automate the habit

points.label: Brain needs water
points.note: Reduces grogginess, sharpens focus

points.label: Reduces sleep inertia
points.note: The 'not quite awake' feeling after sleep

c2_energy_tips.label: Protein in first meal
c2_energy_tips.desc: Protein at breakfast stabilizes blood sugar and prevents the afternoon energy crash.
c2_energy_tips.keyFact: A protein-rich first meal (~25–30g) controls appetite all day by raising GLP-1 and reducing ghrelin more effectively than simple carbohydrates.
c2_energy_tips.detail: Breakfast isn't mandatory for everyone, but if you do eat in the morning, protein is the most important component.
details: A breakfast high in refined carbs (white bread) spikes blood glucose and crashes around 10–11 AM.
25–30g of protein at breakfast slows absorption, stabilizes blood glucose, and maintains satiety through to near lunchtime.
Easy morning protein sources: 3 eggs (~18g), 200g Greek yogurt (~17g), 80g cold chicken breast (~26g).
You don't have to eat breakfast right after waking — many people do fine fasting until 9–10 AM.
Coffee + sugar is not breakfast — it's a short-term cortisol and blood sugar spike that will crash your energy earlier.
Ideal combination: protein + fiber (vegetables, fruit) for your first meal.

points.label: 25–30g protein
points.note: Target for your first meal

points.note: Causes blood sugar crash at 10–11 AM

points.label: No need to eat right away
points.note: Eat when hungry, but include protein

points.note: Eggs, Greek yogurt, cheese

c2_energy_tips.label: Post-meal walk
c2_energy_tips.desc: 5–10 minutes of walking after lunch keeps you alert, prevents post-meal drowsiness, and stabilizes blood sugar.
c2_energy_tips.keyFact: A 10-minute walk after a meal reduces post-meal blood glucose by 22% — more effective than a 30-minute walk at any other time of day.
c2_energy_tips.detail: The post-lunch energy dip is a natural physiological phenomenon — but you can significantly reduce it by moving lightly.
details: After a meal, blood redirects to the digestive system and blood glucose rises — staying seated prolongs this.
Light walking activates muscles to absorb glucose from the blood (without insulin) — just 10 minutes reduces blood glucose significantly.
No need to walk fast — just 'moving' is enough. A loop around the office or 1–2 flights of stairs all have the same effect.
Ideal timing: start walking within 20–30 minutes after finishing your meal.
The post-lunch dip naturally peaks at 1–3 PM — walking + natural light is the most powerful combo to push through.
A short walk outside also resets your thinking, reduces stress, and improves afternoon focus.

points.label: 5–10 min is enough
points.note: No long workout needed

points.label: Within 30 min of eating
points.note: Blood glucose is peaking — best timing

points.label: Reduces blood glucose 22%

c2_energy_tips.label: Smart caffeine
c2_energy_tips.desc: Don't drink caffeine before water or food. Avoid caffeine after 3 PM if you have trouble sleeping.
c2_energy_tips.keyFact: Drinking coffee right after waking when cortisol is at its peak (6–9 AM) wastes caffeine's effect — waiting 90–120 minutes is the optimal window.
c2_energy_tips.detail: Caffeine is a powerful tool when used correctly, and an enemy of sleep when overused.
details: Cortisol peaks 30–45 minutes after waking — drinking coffee at this time adds nothing and increases caffeine tolerance.
Drinking coffee 90–120 minutes after waking delivers maximum and longer-lasting alertness.
Coffee on an empty stomach raises cortisol and stomach acid — drink it after water and a light snack.
Caffeine's half-life is 5–6 hours: a coffee at 3 PM still has 50% caffeine in your bloodstream at 9 PM.
'People who are not caffeine-sensitive' are often still affected in their sleep quality without realizing it.
Practical limit: 1–2 cups of coffee per day, consumed before 2 PM. Green tea and matcha also count.

points.label: Drink 90 min after waking
points.note: Cortisol drops — caffeine finally works

points.note: Avoid empty stomach + dehydration

points.note: Half-life 5–6h lingers into evening

pillarC.c1_desc: Sleep is not 'dead time'. Sleep is when the body repairs muscles, balances hormones, and restores mental health.

c1_checklist.label: Reduce screen time 30+ min before bed
c1_checklist.detail: Blue light from screens suppresses melatonin — the sleep-signaling hormone. Turning off screens 30 minutes before bed is the simplest intervention to improve sleep quality.
c1_checklist.keyFact: Blue light (480nm) suppresses melatonin twice as effectively as regular white light — one hour of screen time at night can delay sleep by 30–45 minutes even after the device is off.
details: Melatonin starts rising 2 hours before your usual bedtime. Screen light during this window disrupts melatonin accumulation, making it harder to feel sleepy.
30 minutes is the minimum — ideally 60 minutes screen-free. But even cutting the last 30 minutes before bed has a measurable impact on sleep onset time.
Practical solutions: enable Night Mode/f.lux from 7–8 PM, dim screen brightness 30–40% after 9 PM. If you must use screens, amber-lens blue-light glasses work better than Night Mode alone.
Replace screens in the last 30 minutes: read a physical book under warm light, journal, meditate lightly, listen to a podcast (without looking at a screen).
Keeping your phone away from the bed (charging in another room) reduces the urge to check it before sleep and during night wakings — two of the most common sleep-disrupting habits.
Success signal: you start feeling sleepy at your target bedtime instead of having to 'force' sleep. Melatonin runs on schedule when not disrupted by blue light.

points.label: Night Mode 7–8 PM
points.note: Earlier than you think you need it

points.label: Book instead of screen
points.note: Warm light doesn't suppress melatonin

points.label: Phone away from bed
points.note: Reduces midnight check-in urge

points.label: Sleepy on time
points.note: Sign that melatonin is working correctly

c1_checklist.label: No caffeine after 3 PM
c1_checklist.detail: Caffeine has a 5–7 hour half-life — a 3 PM coffee still has 50% activity at 8–10 PM, silently degrading deep sleep quality even if you can fall asleep.
c1_checklist.keyFact: Caffeine doesn't just make sleep harder — it reduces slow-wave (deep) sleep by up to 20% even in people who consider themselves 'caffeine insensitive'.
details: Caffeine works by blocking adenosine receptors — adenosine is the 'fatigue molecule' that builds up throughout the day. When caffeine blocks these receptors, the brain doesn't receive sleepiness signals even when the body is genuinely tired.
Half-life of 5–7 hours means: 200 mg caffeine (2 espressos) at 3 PM → 100 mg still active at 8–10 PM. For slow metabolizers (CYP1A2 gene variant), half-life reaches 9–10 hours.
The 3 PM cut-off is safe for most people. If you sleep at 10 PM, caffeine consumed at 3 PM drops to only 25–50 mg by bedtime — below the significant threshold for most people.
Hidden caffeine sources: green tea 25–50 mg/cup, black tea 40–70 mg, dark chocolate 20–30 mg/30 g, energy drinks 80–150 mg, some headache medications contain 65 mg per tablet.

When you need afternoon energy: switch to green tea (L-theanine slows absorption) or take a 10-minute walk — natural light and movement boost alertness as well as 100 mg caffeine without affecting sleep.
If you must have caffeine late: take it with food, choose a lower-caffeine source (matcha over espresso), and accept going to bed 30–45 minutes later that night.

points.label: Cut-off at 3 PM
points.note: Safe for most people sleeping at 10 PM

points.label: CYP1A2 gene
points.note: Slow metabolizers need an earlier cut-off

points.label: Matcha instead of espresso
points.note: L-theanine smooths the caffeine curve

points.label: 10-minute walk
points.note: Equals 100 mg caffeine — no sleep impact

c1_checklist.label: Have a 5–30 min evening routine
c1_checklist.detail: An evening routine is a consistent signal telling the brain it's time to shift into sleep mode — the nervous system needs active wind-down time and can't jump directly from working to sleeping.
c1_checklist.keyFact: The brain needs 20–30 minutes to lower core body temperature and raise melatonin enough to enter deep sleep. Working or consuming stimulating content up to bedtime keeps core temperature and cortisol elevated.
details: Evening routines work through conditioning: when you perform the same sequence of activities before bed each night, the brain learns to associate that sequence with sleepiness. After 2–3 weeks, just starting the routine triggers drowsiness.
Minimum effective time: 5 minutes. Even a short routine (wash face → brush teeth → 1 minute of breathing) creates a transition signal when done consistently every night.

Most effective components: reduce light and noise → personal hygiene → passive relaxation (reading, journaling, light meditation) → breathing. Avoid mentally stimulating activities (problem-solving, planning).
Temperature: a warm shower or bath 1–2 hours before bed paradoxically speeds up sleep — heat draws blood to the skin surface, then dissipates, lowering core body temperature faster.

Journaling 5 minutes before bed (especially writing a to-do list for tomorrow) reduces sleep onset time by an average of 9 minutes (2018 study) — the brain doesn't need to remind itself of tasks during the night.
Start small: pick one 5-minute activity and do it consistently for 7 days before adding another. A simple routine done regularly beats a complex one done occasionally.

points.label: Conditioning
points.note: 2–3 weeks for the brain to learn the link

points.label: Warm shower/bath
points.note: 1–2h before bed lowers core temperature

points.label: Write a to-do list
points.note: Reduces sleep onset time by 9 minutes

points.label: Start with one thing
points.note: 5 consistent minutes beats 30 occasional

c1_checklist.label: Get to bed within your target window
c1_checklist.detail: A consistent bedtime — even if you don't fall asleep immediately — helps your circadian clock learn your sleep time and prepare melatonin at the right moment.
c1_checklist.keyFact: Bed must be the only signal your brain receives: 'this is the place for sleep'. Working, watching movies, or scrolling in bed breaks this association — the brain starts treating bed as a place for wakefulness.
details: Stimulus control therapy (CBT-I): core principle is bed = sleep and sex only, no other activities in bed.

'Target window' means getting into bed within 30 minutes of your goal sleep time. No need to hit exactly 10:30 PM every night, but staying in the 10:00–11:00 PM range is far better than 9 PM one night and 1 AM the next.

If you can't sleep after 20 minutes: get up and do something boring under low light until genuinely sleepy, then return to bed. Lying there restless creates bed-anxiety and makes things worse long-term.
Avoid repaying sleep debt by sleeping in — if you sleep late one night, still wake at your normal time the next day and tolerate drowsiness to rebuild sleep pressure for that evening.
Using your bed only for sleep improves sleep efficiency (ratio of actual sleep to total time in bed). Sleep efficiency below 85% is a sign adjustments are needed.
Making your bed each evening (fluffing the pillow, arranging the blanket) as a routine step acts as a dual trigger: signals the brain and creates a comfortable environment.

points.label: 30-minute window
points.note: No need to be precise to the minute

points.label: Bed = sleep only
points.note: CBT-I stimulus control

points.label: Can't sleep → get up
points.note: After 20 minutes, leave the bed

points.label: Sleep efficiency >85%
points.note: An important quality metric

c1_checklist.label: Sleep enough or better than yesterday
c1_checklist.detail: The most flexible criterion — not requiring immediate perfection but aiming for cumulative improvement. 'Better than yesterday' creates more sustainable momentum than chasing an absolute standard.
c1_checklist.keyFact: 'Enough sleep' is subjective — objective signs: waking up before or at your alarm, no drowsiness before 2 PM, able to focus for 3 hours in the morning without caffeine.
details: 'Or better than yesterday' matters more than 'hit 7 hours'. If you slept 5 hours last night and 5.5 hours tonight — you're moving in the right direction. Gradual progress is more sustainable than sudden change.
Signs of enough sleep (no tracker needed): wake up without needing an alarm; no drowsiness in the 1–2 hours after waking; able to focus for 90 consecutive minutes in the morning without caffeine.

Sleep in 90-minute cycles: each cycle includes light sleep → deep sleep → REM. Waking mid-cycle (e.g., at 4.5 hours) feels worse than waking after 6 hours (4 complete cycles). Aim for multiples of 90 minutes + 15 minutes to fall asleep.
Simple tracking: note your bedtime and wake time each morning (10 seconds). After 1 week, review the pattern and identify what made your best sleep nights happen.

1–2 bad nights of sleep are normal and cause no lasting harm — sleep anxiety (the pressure to 'have to sleep well') is one of the most common causes of chronic insomnia. Accept a bad night and focus on habits, not outcomes.

Short naps (10–20 minutes before 3 PM) can partially compensate for the previous night's sleep loss without affecting evening sleep. Naps over 30 minutes or after 3 PM risk reducing sleep pressure for that evening.

points.label: Incremental progress
points.note: 'Better than yesterday' is more sustainable

points.label: 90-minute multiples
points.note: Calculate sleep time by cycle

points.label: 10-second tracking
points.note: Log sleep/wake time each morning

points.label: Accept a bad night
points.note: Sleep anxiety makes insomnia worse

pillarC.explore_deep_desc: 12 in-depth topics on healthy lifestyle — from sleep science to designing your living environment.
pillarC.assessment_desc: Assess your current lifestyle across 7 important dimensions. Your results will identify which Track you're on and suggest priority actions suited to you.
pillarC.c3_standup_desc: Every 45–60 minutes of sitting, stand up for 2 minutes. Get water, roll your shoulders, stretch, do calf raises. Don't wait until you're in pain to stand up.

c1_steps.title: Fix your sleep/wake schedule
c1_steps.desc: No need to be perfectly precise, but aim to keep variation within 60 minutes across days, including weekends.
c1_steps.keyFact: Going to sleep and waking at the same time each day matters more than total hours slept — consistency is the #1 factor for deep sleep.
c1_steps.detail: Your circadian clock is set primarily by your wake time, not your bedtime. Fixing your wake time is the key to regulating your entire sleep cycle.
details: The brain uses your wake time as an 'anchor' to count back to the natural sleepiness window — which is why waking at the same time matters more than going to bed at the same time.
'Social jet lag' — sleeping late and waking late on weekends — creates an effect equivalent to crossing 2–3 time zones every week for your body.
After 3–4 weeks of consistent wake times, feelings of sleepiness will naturally appear at the right time without any deliberate effort.
No need to force an earlier bedtime right away — just fix your WAKE time first. Your sleep time will self-adjust within 1–2 weeks.
If you're forced to stay up late, still wake at your normal time the next day instead of sleeping in — sleeping in breaks the circadian pattern you're building.
Bright light in the first 30 minutes after waking (go outside or open the curtains) helps 'lock' your wake time into your circadian clock much faster.

points.label: Fixed wake time
points.note: More important than your bedtime

points.label: Including weekends
points.note: ±60 minutes is acceptable

points.label: Light after waking
points.note: Go outside or open curtains for 30 min

points.label: 3–4 weeks to form
points.note: Then natural sleepiness arrives on cue

c1_steps.title: Reduce bright light in the evening
c1_steps.desc: Dim the lights and reduce screens from 9–10 PM. Bright light at night suppresses natural melatonin.
c1_steps.keyFact: Just 10–15 minutes of blue light exposure in the evening is enough to suppress melatonin by 50% for the next 2–3 hours — according to Harvard research.
c1_steps.detail: Melatonin — the hormone that signals 'night is here' — begins to rise about 2 hours before your natural sleep time. Blue light from screens is its number-one enemy.
details: Phone, computer, and TV screens emit blue light (450–490 nm) — the wavelength the brain 'reads' as daytime and uses to block melatonin production.
Blue-light filtering glasses or Night Mode reduces blue light by roughly 20–30% — helpful but not a complete solution.
Dimming home lights from 9 PM and switching to warm amber light (<3000K) sends a 'night is coming' signal to the brain far more effectively than any color-filter app.
Reading a paper book instead of a screen 30 minutes before bed cuts average time to fall asleep by 12 minutes and improves sleep quality.
Wearing blue-light blocking glasses (amber lens) from 8 PM is the most effective solution if you must use screens late for work.
Ambient room lighting (bright overhead lights) has more impact than a small phone screen — prioritize darkening the room before worrying about Night Mode.

points.label: Dim lights from 9 PM
points.note: Switch to warm light <3000K

points.note: Or use blue-light-blocking glasses

points.note: Replace screens for 30 min before bed

points.note: Enable from 7–8 PM, not just at bedtime

c1_steps.title: Reduce physical stimulation
c1_steps.desc: Avoid caffeine after 2–3 PM, avoid intense exercise close to bedtime, and avoid stressful work right before sleep.
c1_steps.keyFact: Caffeine has a half-life of 5–6 hours: a coffee at 3 PM still has 50% of its active compounds in your blood at 9 PM — enough to disrupt deep sleep even if you can fall asleep.
c1_steps.detail: Stimulation from caffeine, heavy exercise, or stressful work creates a physiological environment that is the opposite of what your body needs to enter deep sleep.
details: Caffeine works by blocking adenosine receptors — adenosine is the sleepiness-accumulating molecule. When caffeine wears off, adenosine 'floods back', causing sudden fatigue.
Caffeine-sensitive people: drinks with caffeine after noon are enough to affect sleep — this is genetic, not a sign of weak willpower.
Heavy training within 2–3 hours of bedtime raises cortisol and core body temperature — both make it harder to sleep. Light exercise (walking, yoga) is fine.
Stressful work before sleep activates the brain's 'problem-solving mode' — the sympathetic nervous system stays active even after you close your laptop.
'Wind-down' 30–60 minutes: stop email/work, do light activities requiring no decisions. The brain needs time to shift from 'fight mode' to 'rest mode'.
Alcohol helps you fall asleep faster but disrupts REM and deep sleep in the second half of the night — overall sleep quality is significantly worse.

points.label: Cut caffeine after 2–3 PM
points.note: 5–6 hour half-life stays in your blood

points.label: Light exercise near bedtime
points.note: Walking/yoga OK, heavy training — no

points.label: Stop work at 9 PM
points.note: Wind-down 30–60 min before sleep

points.label: Limit evening alcohol
points.note: Disrupts REM though it helps you fall asleep

c1_steps.title: Optimize your bedroom
c1_steps.desc: Dark, cool (~18–21°C), quiet. Use the bed mainly for sleeping — not for working or watching videos.
c1_steps.keyFact: A room temperature of 18–21°C is the optimal condition for deep sleep — your core body temperature needs to drop 1–2°C to enter deep sleep.
c1_steps.detail: The bedroom is an environment that triggers sleep behavior. When the brain associates bed with work, screens, or stress, it stops reading 'bed = sleep' as a signal.
details: A cooler room helps you sleep more deeply because your brain and body need to lower their temperature to enter deep sleep (NREM stage 3).
Complete (or near-complete) darkness matters more than many people think: street light through thin curtains is enough to reduce sleep quality.
'Stimulus control': the bed is only for sleeping and intimacy — no working, no watching movies, no scrolling social media in bed.
Intermittent noise (traffic, voices) disrupts sleep more than continuous background noise — white noise or a gentle fan can help mask intermittent sounds.
Mattress and pillow quality affect sleep posture and morning aches — this is the most worthwhile bedroom investment if you wake up in pain.
Keeping your bedroom tidy reduces 'visual noise' — research shows cluttered rooms are associated with difficulty falling asleep and lighter sleep.

points.label: 18–21°C
points.note: Optimal temperature for deep sleep

points.label: Complete darkness
points.note: Blackout curtains or sleep mask

c3_levels.label: Beginner
c3_levels.keyFact: Adding just 1,000 steps/day above your current level already reduces cardiovascular disease risk by 10% and early mortality by 15% — even the smallest goal has clear benefits.
c3_levels.detail: The best starting point is not 10,000 steps — it's anywhere above your current level. The body responds to change, not to absolute numbers.
details: First measure your baseline: wear your phone or smartwatch for 3–5 days without changing habits, and record your actual average.
Increase by 1,000–2,000 steps above THAT baseline — not compared to 'someone else's 10,000 goal'. If you walk 2,000 steps now, aim for 3,000–4,000.
Studies confirm health benefits begin with the very first small increase — creating an upward trend matters more than jumping to a big number.
At this stage, you don't need to track precisely every day — just feeling 'I moved more than usual today' is a success.
Add 1 small habit: walk after a meal, take 1 flight of stairs, park one spot further. Each small habit adds roughly 200–500 steps.
After 2–3 weeks your baseline rises naturally — then increase by another 500–1,000 steps rather than holding the same target.

points.label: Measure baseline first
points.note: Track 3–5 days without changing habits

points.label: +1,000–2,000 increase
points.note: Compared to your own baseline

points.label: Increase every 2–3 weeks
points.note: Don't jump too fast

points.label: Small habits add up
points.note: 200–500 steps per habit

c3_levels.label: Basic
c3_levels.keyFact: 7,000 steps/day reduces early mortality risk by 50–70% compared to under 2,000 steps — this is the largest single 'inflection point' in the step-count research.
c3_levels.detail: The 6,000–8,000 range offers the best health benefit per time invested — enough for significant impact without needing dedicated walking sessions.
details: JAMA Internal Medicine 2019 study of 16,741 women: 7,500 steps/day reduced early mortality by 65% vs. the 2,700-step group. Benefits plateau around 7,500–8,000 steps.
At this level you don't need separate walking sessions — distributed movement throughout the day (office walking, stairs, errands) is enough.
6,000–8,000 steps equals roughly 45–60 minutes of accumulated movement — completely achievable on a busy schedule.
This is the most sustainable level long-term without feeling like a task — challenging enough but not overwhelming.
Track weekly rather than daily: a 7-day average matters more than hitting the exact target every day.
Once you consistently hit this level for 3–4 weeks, your body adapts — 6,000 steps will feel easy and natural.

points.label: 7,000 steps = inflection point
points.note: Reduces early mortality risk 50–70%

points.label: 45–60 min accumulated
points.note: No need to walk all at once

points.label: Track weekly average
points.note: More flexible than daily tracking

points.label: Maintain 3–4 weeks
points.note: Then it becomes automatic

c3_levels.label: Healthier
c3_levels.keyFact: The 10,000 steps/day figure originates from a 1965 Japanese marketing campaign — actual science shows maximum benefits are achieved at around 8,000–9,000 steps.
c3_levels.detail: 8,000–10,000 steps brings clear improvements in cardiovascular endurance, weight management, and mood. This is the level to 'get healthier', not just 'avoid disease'.
details: The 10,000 steps target was created by Yamasa in 1965 when they launched the 'Manpo-kei' (万歩計) pedometer. No science backed that number at the time.
Modern research shows health benefits increase most sharply from 0→7,000 steps, and continue increasing more slowly from 7,000→10,000 steps.
At 8,000–10,000 steps you begin seeing improvements in: more stable weight, deeper sleep, better mood, and increased endurance.
To reach this naturally: 1 morning or evening walk of 20–30 minutes plus distributed movement throughout the day is enough.
Brisk walking (you can talk but breathing is faster) creates more cardiovascular benefit than slow walking with the same step count.
At this level, quality starts to matter: occasionally walking on uneven terrain or uphill adds extra cardiovascular challenge.

points.label: 20–30 min walk
points.note: + distributed movement all day

points.label: Brisk walk
points.note: Faster pace with elevated heart rate is better

points.label: Quality > quantity
points.note: Hilly terrain adds extra challenge

points.label: 8,000–9,000 is optimal
points.note: 10,000 is marketing, not science

c3_levels.label: Athletic
c3_levels.desc: Personalized according to your recovery capacity
c3_levels.keyFact: People training 4–5 days/week at high intensity may need fewer steps because the body already receives enough movement stimulus — forcing more steps during recovery can slow progress.
c3_levels.detail: When you're already following a structured training program, NEAT must be balanced with recovery needs — it's not 'more is always better'. Listening to your body matters more than hitting a step count.
details: Heavy trainers may need to adjust step goals by training schedule: after a heavy leg day → reduce walking for muscle recovery; on easy days → increase steps.
Signs you need to reduce NEAT: resting heart rate 5–7 bpm higher than usual, training performance declining over 2–3 consecutive sessions, muscle soreness lasting 72+ hours.
For gym-goers, 'active recovery' light walking (3,000–5,000 easy steps) the day after heavy training is often better than complete rest.
Total weekly training load includes gym sessions + NEAT — when training heavily, naturally reducing NEAT a little is the body's intelligent self-regulation.
For competitors or those training 5–6 days/week: alternating high-load weeks with low-load deload weeks leads to better long-term progress.
Tracking tool: morning heart rate variability (HRV) is the best indicator of whether to increase or decrease total daily movement.

points.label: Balance training + NEAT
points.note: Don't force steps during recovery

points.label: Morning HRV
points.note: Best indicator of recovery status

points.label: High/low load weeks
points.note: Periodic deload for long-term progress
