c_circ_light_rules.tip: Use warm lighting, lower screen brightness. Enable Night Mode on devices from 8 PM.
c_circ_light_rules.keyFact: Dimming light below 50 lux (equivalent to candlelight) from 8 PM helps the pineal gland begin secreting melatonin. The body cannot distinguish 'white LED at night' from 'daytime'. These 2 hours are the most important for preparing for deep sleep.
c_circ_light_rules.detail: The human visual system evolved in an environment of campfire and moonlight — warm, dim light with no blue light. Modern LED lighting (especially white light 5,000K+) completely disrupts these biological signals.
details: Melanopsin in retinal cells is most sensitive to 480nm (blue) light — precisely the most common wavelength in white LED lights and modern device screens.
The threshold of <50 lux (equivalent to candlelight) is the minimum for the pineal gland to begin secreting melatonin — typical room lighting is 200–500 lux, well above this threshold.
Warm 2,700–3,000K bulbs (yellow/amber) contain less 480nm light than daytime white bulbs (5,000–6,500K) — the most practical and effective replacement.
Night Mode / True Tone on phones and laptops reduces blue light but does NOT eliminate it completely — still better than nothing, but not equivalent to turning off the screen.
Bathrooms are the biggest weak point: bright white LED at 10 PM destroys accumulated melatonin — install a small warm nightlight for nighttime use.
Smart bulbs scheduled to automatically dim to 2,700K at 8 PM — invest once, applied automatically without needing to remember.

c_circ_light_rules.tip: Bedroom completely dark. Even small indicator lights can affect deep sleep quality.
c_circ_light_rules.keyFact: Even dim 10-lux light (indicator lights, street light through windows) while sleeping reduces deep sleep (N3 and N4) quality. A completely dark bedroom is the most important environmental setup — simple yet rarely done correctly.
c_circ_light_rules.detail: Northwestern University research (2022) found that sleeping in a room with moderate light (100 lux) increases heart rate, raises sleep-time insulin resistance, and significantly reduces deep sleep quality — even when the sleeper is unaware of the light.
details: 10 lux of light in the bedroom (equivalent to a small indicator light or streetlight through thin curtains) is enough to partially suppress melatonin and reduce deep sleep.
Skin and closed eyes can still perceive light through eyelids — the nervous system doesn't fully 'turn off' vision during sleep, especially ipRGC remain sensitive.
Simplest solution: blackout curtains (block street lights, moonlight) + cover all small indicator lights (router, TV standby, phone chargers).
Sleep mask is the most effective and affordable solution — especially useful when traveling, as hotel rooms often have LED indicator lights that can't be turned off.
Smoke detectors, WiFi router lights, TV standby lights: put black tape over them or face them toward the wall — alarms still work, only the light is blocked.
Dark + cool (18–20°C) + quiet bedroom is the optimal environmental trio for deep sleep — lacking any one element reduces recovery effectiveness.

c_circ_caffeine.rule: Don't drink right after waking up
c_circ_caffeine.time: Don't drink right after waking up
c_circ_caffeine.reason: Natural cortisol is already high at 6–8 AM. Caffeine then is less effective and may cause dependence.
c_circ_caffeine.good: Drink 90–120 min after waking (8–9 AM if you wake at 6 AM)
c_circ_caffeine.keyFact: Natural cortisol peaks in the first 30–60 min after waking. Drinking coffee right then is wasteful (cortisol already does caffeine's job) and trains the brain that caffeine = alertness — the foundation of dependence.
c_circ_caffeine.detail: Caffeine dependence starts here: when you drink coffee right after waking every day, the brain reduces natural morning cortisol production and upregulates adenosine receptors — eventually you need caffeine just to feel 'normal', not to become more alert.
details: Cortisol awakening response (CAR) rises 50–100% in the first 30–60 minutes after waking — this is the strongest natural stimulant the brain produces each morning.

Caffeine works by blocking adenosine receptors (which cause drowsiness). When cortisol is high, adenosine is already naturally suppressed — caffeine has little 'room' to act, its effectiveness is clearly reduced.
Drinking coffee right after waking every day causes the brain to reduce morning cortisol production over time — you need caffeine just to feel normal, not to become more alert.
Waiting 90–120 minutes after waking (when cortisol starts to fall) is when caffeine is most effective — you use less but feel a stronger effect.
In the first 90 min: drink water (250–500ml), get outside for light, eat a light protein snack — these provide alertness comparable to coffee without causing dependence.
14-day challenge: no coffee before 9 AM — after 2 weeks, most people report better morning alertness and less need for caffeine throughout the day.

c_circ_caffeine.rule: Don't drink on an empty stomach
c_circ_caffeine.time: Don't drink on an empty stomach
c_circ_caffeine.phase: Drink after a light protein snack

c_circ_caffeine.good: Drink after drinking water and eating a light protein snack
c_circ_caffeine.keyFact: Caffeine on an empty stomach directly stimulates stomach acid production and raises cortisol further — causing rapid heartbeat, anxiety, stomach irritation, and accelerates the brain's craving for caffeine.
c_circ_caffeine.detail: Food (especially protein) slows caffeine absorption into the bloodstream — instead of a quick spike then crash, you get a smoother and longer-lasting energy curve. This is why drinking coffee after breakfast feels better and more sustained than before.
details: Caffeine on an empty stomach is absorbed 45% faster into the bloodstream — creating a sudden cortisol spike and increased stomach acid, causing irritation, mild nausea, or rapid heartbeat in sensitive people.
Protein food (eggs, dairy, legumes) slows caffeine absorption — a smoother energy curve with no sudden crash after 2–3 hours.
Caffeine on an empty stomach additionally raises cortisol — if you're already stressed in the morning, coffee when hungry can push cortisol to levels causing anxiety or restlessness.
Drink water before coffee (at least 250ml): mild dehydration after sleep amplifies the negative effects of caffeine on an empty stomach.
If you can't eat breakfast: at minimum drink a glass of water and eat a handful of nuts or a boiled egg before coffee — enough to reduce the negative impact.
Bulletproof coffee (blended with butter/coconut oil) is a solution for those who eat late — fat slows absorption similarly to food, reducing cortisol spike.

c_circ_caffeine.reason: Caffeine half-life ~5–6 hours. Drinking at 3 PM → half remains at 9 PM → harder to fall asleep.
c_circ_caffeine.good: Sensitive people: cut off after noon–1 PM
c_circ_caffeine.keyFact: Caffeine's half-life is 5–6 hours — drinking 1 cup of coffee at 3 PM leaves half the caffeine in your bloodstream at 9 PM when you need to fall asleep. Caffeine doesn't make you 'awake', it blocks adenosine — which still accumulates masked, causing hidden sleep debt.
c_circ_caffeine.detail: Many people drink afternoon coffee and still fall asleep — but sleep poorly. Remaining caffeine reduces slow-wave sleep (N3) by up to 20% even when you sleep enough hours. You sleep a sufficient number of hours but don't recover adequately.
details: Caffeine's average half-life is 5–6 hours, but varies from 3–9 hours depending on the CYP1A2 gene — 50% of the population are 'slow metabolizers' who need an additional 2–3 hours for full clearance.
Drinking 200mg caffeine (1 large coffee) at 3 PM → 100mg remaining at 9 PM → 50mg at 3 AM — equivalent to half an espresso in your bloodstream while sleeping.
Caffeine reduces slow-wave sleep (deep sleep N3) by up to 20% even when you sleep 7–8 full hours — you sleep enough hours but don't recover enough, waking still tired.
Adenosine accumulates throughout the day but is blocked by caffeine — when caffeine wears off at night, adenosine suddenly floods in, causing extreme fatigue in the late afternoon.
Personal test: try cutting off after 1 PM for 1 week and note sleep quality. If clearly improved, you're a slow metabolizer — need to cut off earlier.
After-2-PM alternatives: green tea (less caffeine ~30mg, with L-theanine to smooth the effect), cold drinks, a short walk — enough to break the post-lunch dip without disrupting sleep.

c_circ_caffeine.rule: Don't use it to mask sleep deprivation
c_circ_caffeine.time: Don't use it to mask sleep deprivation
c_circ_caffeine.phase: Good sleep + less caffeine > less sleep + more caffeine
c_circ_caffeine.reason: Caffeine cannot replace sleep. It only blocks the feeling of tiredness, it does not restore cognitive function.
c_circ_caffeine.good: Good sleep + less caffeine > less sleep + more caffeine
c_circ_caffeine.keyFact: Caffeine blocks adenosine receptors — masking the feeling of fatigue but NOT restoring cognitive performance. Sleep-deprived people with lots of caffeine still make decisions as poorly as intoxicated people, but don't feel that way. This is the most dangerous 'alertness illusion'.
c_circ_caffeine.detail: Research by Matthew Walker (Why We Sleep) and groups at Harvard shows caffeine can mask subjective sleepiness but cannot improve reaction time, working memory, or decision-making of sleep-deprived people — these functions can only be restored by actual sleep.
details: Caffeine blocks adenosine receptors but adenosine keeps accumulating — when caffeine wears off, all the adenosine floods in at once, causing a stronger 'crash' than normal.
Chronically sleep-deprived people (<6h/night) accumulate 'sleep debt' that caffeine cannot repay — the brain loses its ability to accurately recognize its own fatigue level.
Good sleep + 1 morning coffee > poor sleep + 3–4 coffees/day — by every measure: productivity, memory, decisions, long-term health.
Caffeine cannot restore: memory consolidation (only happens during deep N3 sleep), emotional regulation (REM sleep), motor learning, immune function.
'Caffeine nap' is the only truly valid exception: drink coffee → sleep 20 min right away → caffeine absorbs exactly when you wake up = real alertness for 2–3 hours.
Signs you're using caffeine to mask sleep deprivation: needing >3 cups/day to feel normal, can't function morning after without coffee, falling asleep immediately when sitting still.

c_circ_post_lunch.solution: This is a normal biological cycle at 1–3 PM. A 10–20 min nap is more effective than coffee.
c_circ_post_lunch.keyFact: Adenosine — the sleep-inducing molecule — accumulates since waking and reaches a sufficient threshold to cause clear drowsiness at 1–3 PM, coinciding with a natural circadian dip. This is not your fault — it's biological design.
c_circ_post_lunch.detail: Two factors combine to create the post-lunch dip: (1) sleep pressure from adenosine accumulated since morning, and (2) a natural circadian dip at 1–3 PM — even people who skip lunch experience this. A high-carb meal just makes it worse.
details: Adenosine accumulates in the brain from the moment you wake — concentration rises steadily with each waking hour. By 1–3 PM it's high enough to cause clear drowsiness even without eating lunch.
The circadian rhythm has two natural daily dips: 2–4 AM and 1–3 PM — this is an evolutionary result, not a bad habit.
A 10–20 minute power nap (not more than 30 min) clears some adenosine without entering deep sleep — you wake up alert without 'sleep inertia'.
If you sleep more than 30 minutes: you enter deeper sleep (N2/N3) — you wake up with strong sleep inertia, taking 20–30 minutes to be fully alert.
'Caffeine nap': drink coffee → sleep 20 min immediately → caffeine absorbs exactly when you wake — combines two effects, more alertness than either alone.
No conditions for sleep: 10–15 min meditation, 4-7-8 breathing, or simply closing your eyes without stimulation also helps partially reduce adenosine pressure.

points.note: Accumulates since morning, enough to cause drowsiness at 1–3 PM

c_circ_post_lunch.solution: Eating lots of fast carbs → blood sugar spike then crash → drowsiness. Fix: add protein + vegetables.
c_circ_post_lunch.keyFact: A lunch heavy in fast carbohydrates (white rice, bread, sugary drinks) causes a blood sugar spike then rapid crash — triggering strong insulin release and increasing tryptophan into the brain → serotonin → melatonin. This is a food-amplified post-lunch dip.
c_circ_post_lunch.detail: It's not rice causing drowsiness — it's the macro ratio: white rice without accompanying protein and fiber. The same amount of carbs combined with protein + fiber will cause a slower, steadier blood sugar rise with no sudden crash afterward.
details: High-GI carbs cause rapid blood sugar rise → pancreas secretes lots of insulin → blood sugar crashes → brain signals 'glucose shortage' → drowsiness and difficulty concentrating.
Post-meal insulin surge also drives tryptophan into the brain → converted to serotonin → partly to melatonin — explains why drowsiness is stronger after a large meal.
Simple fix: add protein (meat, fish, beans, eggs) and fiber (green vegetables) to lunch — slows glucose absorption, steadier blood sugar, no crash.
Reduce rice portion by 30% + add equivalent vegetables and protein: post-meal blood sugar significantly lower without feeling hungrier.
Sugary drinks, fruit juice (even 100% natural) at lunch: liquid glucose absorbed faster than solid food — avoid or replace with plain water.
Ideal lunch for afternoon energy: ½ plate vegetables + ¼ protein + ¼ complex carbs (brown rice, sweet potato) — steady blood sugar for 3–4 hours.

c_circ_post_lunch.solution: Walking 5–10 min after lunch improves alertness and stabilizes blood sugar better than coffee.
c_circ_post_lunch.keyFact: A 10-minute walk after eating reduces the blood sugar spike by up to 30% and sustains stable glucose levels longer — more effective than 30 minutes of pre-meal exercise. This is the simplest 'hack' with the best cost-to-benefit ratio.
c_circ_post_lunch.detail: Muscles contracting during walking directly consume glucose without needing insulin — reducing the load on the pancreas and preventing excessive post-meal blood sugar spikes. Combined with natural light and an upright posture, post-meal walking is one of the most evidence-backed habits.
details: Contracting muscles during walking consume glucose through an insulin-independent mechanism (GLUT4 translocation) — quickly and effectively lowering the post-meal blood sugar peak.
Research from George Washington University: walking 15 minutes after each meal controls blood sugar better than a single 45-minute walk per day — less total time but more effective.
Standing and walking posture helps the digestive system work better than sitting: gravity aids food movement through the gut and reduces pressure on the diaphragm.
Natural light during a 5–10 min lunch walk also helps maintain the afternoon circadian rhythm — reducing the risk of premature melatonin secretion.
No space to walk: standing in place or doing seated heel raises also activates leg muscles — less effective but has a measurable impact.
After 10 minutes of walking: steadier blood sugar, the brain receives a consistent glucose supply instead of a spike then crash — focus sustained 45–60 minutes longer.

c_circ_post_lunch.solution: Mild dehydration (1–2%) causes fatigue. Drink 200–300ml of water before and after lunch.
c_circ_post_lunch.keyFact: Losing just 1–2% of body weight in water is enough to reduce cognitive performance by 5–10% and cause noticeable fatigue — below the thirst threshold. You become dehydrated before you feel thirsty.
c_circ_post_lunch.detail: Many people confuse midday fatigue with hunger or drowsiness when the real cause is mild dehydration accumulated since morning. The brain is 73% water — the organ most sensitive to dehydration.
details: 1% water loss (700ml for a 70kg person) measurably reduces concentration and information processing speed — this threshold is typically reached before lunch if you haven't been drinking since morning.
The feeling of thirst only appears around 1.5–2% dehydration — meaning by the time you feel thirsty, cognitive performance has already declined.
The brain is 73% water and consumes 20% of the body's water — the organ most sensitive to dehydration, explaining why water deficiency causes mental fatigue more noticeably than physical fatigue.
Drink 200–300ml before lunch and 200ml after: provides sufficient water for digestion and replenishes fluid lost through breathing and sweating since morning.
Plain water is most effective — sparkling water, juice, and coffee do NOT fully replace plain water for hydration purposes.
Signs of adequate hydration: pale yellow urine (like straw) — dark yellow = drink more immediately; clear = drinking more than needed.

c_circ_tracker.keyFact: Morning energy is the most sensitive indicator of the previous night's sleep quality. One night of deep, sufficient sleep → naturally alert in the morning. Insufficient deep sleep → groggy even if you slept enough hours.
c_circ_tracker.detail: Morning (7–9 AM) is the 'starting point' of the energy map. Recording your energy level and what you ate/did helps identify which morning habits actually help you feel more alert — and which habits are dragging your energy down.
details: Rate energy 1–5 at 8–9 AM: 1 = very groggy, 3 = normal, 5 = fully alert, no need for coffee. Consistently low scores (1–2) after 7+ hours of sleep = signal of poor deep sleep quality.
Note 'What did you eat?': protein breakfast (eggs, dairy) → energy usually stable until lunch. Sweet bread/fast carbs → blood sugar spikes then crashes before 10 AM.
Note 'What did you do?': morning walk or natural light → morning energy score is typically 1–2 points higher than staying in a dark room.
Compare morning score with last night's sleep time: pattern usually clear after 3–4 days — sleeping before 11 PM → next morning score higher than sleeping after midnight.
Note caffeine: drinking right after waking (before 8 AM) vs waiting until 8–9 AM — record which approach gives more sustained morning energy.
Pattern to watch: if morning score is always ≤ 2 despite 7+ hours of sleep, sleep may be shallow due to: alcohol the evening before, room too bright/warm, or inconsistent sleep schedule.

c_circ_tracker.keyFact: Midday (11 AM–1 PM) is the highest-energy time of day for most people. Record your energy BEFORE lunch — after eating, the score will shift due to the post-lunch dip. Comparing both scores tells you how much your lunch is affecting afternoon energy.
c_circ_tracker.detail: The 11 AM score is the true circadian peak — unaffected by food. The 1 PM score reflects the impact of lunch. Large gap (e.g., 5 down to 2) = lunch was high in fast carbs. Small gap (5 down to 4) = well-balanced lunch.
details: Record score at 11 AM (BEFORE eating): this is the true circadian score, reflecting internal energy not affected by food. This score is typically the highest of the day.
Record score at 1 PM (AFTER eating): compare with 11 AM — a large gap (≥ 2 points) shows lunch is causing a stronger post-lunch dip than normal.
Note 'What did you eat?': white rice + few vegetables/protein → large gap. Brown rice + lots of vegetables + protein → smaller gap. Pattern usually clear after 3–5 days.
Note 'What did you do?': if at 11 AM you were handling unimportant email — you're 'wasting' your cognitive peak. Schedule your most important task at 9–11 AM instead.
If the 11 AM score is always only 3–4 (never reaching 5): review deep sleep quality, caffeine schedule, or chronic stress lowering your energy ceiling.
Compare midday scores across days of the week: many people report Monday scores lower (weekend sleep recovery shifts rhythm) and Friday scores higher (rhythm stable all week).

c_circ_tracker.keyFact: Afternoon (2–4 PM) is the recovery period after the post-lunch dip and entry into the second wind. Afternoon score depends heavily on: (1) whether lunch had protein/vegetables, (2) whether you had a short rest after lunch, (3) whether caffeine cut-off timing was right.
c_circ_tracker.detail: The true second wind begins around 3 PM when body temperature peaks — this is the second-best opportunity of the day for important work. Many people miss it because the post-lunch dip drags on too long due to an unsuitable lunch.
details: Record score at 3 PM: if still ≤ 2 after a good lunch → this is a normal circadian post-lunch dip. If still ≤ 2 after a balanced lunch + short rest → review nighttime sleep quality.
Note 'What did you do at 2–3 PM?': power nap 10–20 min → afternoon score typically 1–2 points higher than without resting. Caffeine nap → often 2+ points higher.
Note caffeine: what time did you drink coffee and what was the afternoon score? Caffeine's effect on evening score and sleep quality usually becomes clear after 5–7 days of tracking.
Compare afternoon score with lunch composition: days eating fewer carbs + more protein/vegetables → afternoon score typically 1 point higher with recovery 30–60 min faster.
Note exercise: if training at 3–5 PM, record score before and after — many people report afternoon training scores significantly higher and sustained through the evening.
Pattern to watch: afternoon score always ≤ 2 despite a good lunch + short rest = sign of accumulated sleep debt — need to sleep 30–60 minutes earlier for 3–5 consecutive nights.

c_circ_tracker.keyFact: The ideal evening score (6–8 PM) is 2–3/5 — naturally declining, no longer at an energy peak but not yet exhausted. Too high (4–5) = overstimulated, hard to fall asleep. Too low (≤ 1) = exhausted, accumulated sleep debt.
c_circ_tracker.detail: The evening score is the best predictor of that night's sleep quality. A consistently stable score of 2–3 across multiple days = circadian rhythm functioning well. Wildly varying scores = unstable circadian rhythm — review sleep/wake times and evening light.
details: Ideal evening score is 2–3: the body is naturally 'landing' — enough energy for social interaction, cooking, light stretching, but no longer enough for heavy work.
Evening score 4–5: overstimulated — usually from high-intensity exercise after 7 PM, late caffeine, stressful news, arguments. Predicts difficulty falling asleep that night.
Evening score ≤ 1: exhausted — usually from accumulated sleep debt. This is a signal to sleep earlier, not to drink more coffee tomorrow morning.
Note 'What did you do 6–8 PM?': action movies/news → evening score usually higher and harder to sleep. Light walking/family conversation/reading → score declines naturally.
Note lighting: warm lights + reducing screens from 8 PM → evening score usually ≤ 3 at 9 PM. Bright lights + screens → score higher and delayed by 1–2 hours.
After 7 days: compare evening score with next morning score — pattern usually clear: evening 2–3 → next morning 4–5. Evening 5 → next morning 2–3.

c_morning_hero.title: Morning Routine

c_sleep_hero.title: Sleep Science
c_sleep_hero.desc: Sleep is not dead time. It is when your body repairs muscle tissue, balances hormones, consolidates memory, and prepares energy for tomorrow.

pillarC.c_sleep_s1_sub: Want lasting health? Don't just train harder — sleep better.
pillarC.c_sleep_s2_sub: A complete sleep cycle lasts ~90 minutes and repeats 4–6 times per night.
pillarC.c_sleep_s2_note: Important note: Deep sleep (N3) is most abundant in the first 3 hours of the night. REM is most abundant in the early morning. Sleeping late → losing deep sleep; waking early → losing REM.
pillarC.c_sleep_s3_sub: Don't force perfect sleep — build an environment that makes sleep easier.
pillarC.c_sleep_s4_sub: Don't shift bedtime too aggressively at once. Every 2–3 days, pull it 15–30 minutes earlier so your body adapts.
pillarC.c_sleep_s5_sub: The 3 most common scenarios and practical solutions.
pillarC.c_sleep_s6_sub: You don't need 5/5 every day. 3/5 is already great for beginners.
c_sleep_checklist: Reduce screen time 30+ minutes before bed
A short evening routine of at least 5 minutes (stretching, breathing, reading)
Get into bed within your target window
Slept as long or better than yesterday
c_sleep_doctor: Insomnia lasting more than 3–4 weeks despite applying sleep hygiene
Sleeping 7–9 hours but still fatigued all day (may be sleep apnea)
Loud snoring or breathing pauses during sleep
Sleepwalking or unusual behaviors during sleep
pillarC.c_sleep_timing_note: ✦ N3 is most abundant in the first 3 hours of the night — REM is most abundant in the early morning. Changing sleep/wake time affects each stage very differently.
pillarC.c_sleep_timing_desc: Not all sleep hours are equal. The body follows a circadian biological clock — N3 and REM have natural 'time windows'. Understanding this helps you optimize sleep not just by hours but also by timing.
c_sleep_timing_details: N3 (deep sleep) is most concentrated in the first 3–4 hours after falling asleep — this is the 'golden window' for physical recovery.
REM is most concentrated in the last 2–3 hours before waking — the early morning 4–7 AM is the longest REM stage.
Sleeping 2 hours late (2 AM instead of midnight) doesn't reduce total sleep time but removes almost all N3.
Waking 2 hours earlier (5 AM instead of 7 AM) doesn't reduce N3 much but loses most important REM.
The same 6 hours of sleep but 11 PM–5 AM (more N3, less REM) is completely different from 1 AM–7 AM (less N3, more REM).
Ideal target: sleep 10–11 PM, wake 6–7 AM — optimizes both N3 (early night) and REM (early morning).

c_sleep_facts.label: Muscle Recovery
c_sleep_facts.desc: During deep sleep (slow-wave sleep), the body secretes GH — the growth hormone that repairs muscle tissue after training.
c_sleep_facts.keyFact: 95% of Growth Hormone (GH) is released during N3 deep sleep — insufficient sleep means insufficient GH, and muscle tissue is not repaired no matter how much you train.
c_sleep_facts.detail: Deep sleep (slow-wave sleep, N3) is the body's 'repair workshop'. This is where GH is most strongly secreted — stimulating protein synthesis, repairing micro-damage to muscles after training, and regenerating connective tissue. Skip sleep = skip most of your training gains.
details: Growth hormone GH is secreted 70–80% during N3 (deep sleep) within the first 1–2 hours after falling asleep.
GH stimulates muscle protein synthesis — the process of converting amino acids into new muscle tissue.
Just one night of poor sleep can reduce muscle protein synthesis by 18% — a significant reduction in training effectiveness.
Cortisol (the muscle-breakdown hormone) rises when you sleep poorly — this is why heavy training with poor sleep produces no results.
Besides GH, insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) also rises during deep sleep — supporting bone and tendon recovery.
7–9 consecutive hours of sleep is more important than multiple short naps — N3 occurs mainly in the first 4 hours of sleep.

c_sleep_facts.label: Memory Enhancement
c_sleep_facts.desc: The brain consolidates information learned during the day. Poor sleep reduces the ability to learn new skills and recover motor technique.
c_sleep_facts.keyFact: During REM sleep, the brain 'replays' skills learned during the day — this is why sleeping after learning helps remember 40% better than staying awake.
c_sleep_facts.detail: The brain doesn't 'turn off' during sleep — it's busy 'saving files'. During N2 (sleep spindles) and REM, the hippocampus transfers short-term information to the cortex for long-term storage. This is memory consolidation — poor sleep disrupts this process.
details: Memory consolidation occurs in 2 stages: N2 (motor skills, procedural memory) and REM (factual knowledge, declarative memory).
Sleep spindles in N2 actively transfer information from the hippocampus (short-term) to the neocortex (long-term).
REM sleep is especially important for motor skills — learning a new movement requires sleep for the brain to consolidate motor memory.
One poor night of sleep reduces ability to learn new words by 40% and new skill retention by 30%.
A 20–30 minute power nap contains enough N2 to significantly improve learning performance afterward.
'Sleep to forget' — REM also helps discard unnecessary information, keeping the brain from becoming overloaded.

points.note: REM replays learned skills — remember 40% longer

c_sleep_facts.label: Hunger Hormone Control
c_sleep_facts.desc: Poor sleep increases ghrelin (hunger hormone) and decreases leptin (satiety hormone). People who sleep poorly tend to crave sweets and high-calorie foods more.
c_sleep_facts.keyFact: Just 2 nights of sleeping 2 fewer hours than needed increases ghrelin by 28% and decreases leptin by 18% — equivalent to the hunger of skipping 1,000 kcal.
c_sleep_facts.detail: Ghrelin and leptin are 2 hormones controlling hunger and fullness. Poor sleep severely disrupts this balance: ghrelin rises (you feel hungrier), leptin falls (you don't feel full even after eating enough). This biological mechanism explains why people who sleep less tend to eat more and gain weight more easily.
details: Ghrelin (hunger hormone) is produced mainly in the stomach — rises before meals to signal the need for energy.
Leptin (satiety hormone) is secreted from fat tissue — rises after eating and during sleep to signal fullness and suppress eating.
Just 2 nights of 4 hours of sleep: ghrelin up 28%, leptin down 18%, and participants self-reported 24% more hunger.
People who sleep less tend to crave refined carbohydrates, sweets and high-calorie foods — the brain seeks quick energy.
High cortisol from poor sleep also increases insulin resistance — the body struggles to process blood sugar, craving sweets even more.
Fix: sleeping 7–9 hours is a free 'nutritional intervention' to help control food cravings.

c_sleep_facts.label: Cardiovascular Health
c_sleep_facts.desc: Adequate sleep helps lower blood pressure, reduce inflammation, and balance heart rate. Sleeping under 6 hours significantly increases cardiovascular risk.
c_sleep_facts.keyFact: People who sleep less than 6 hours per night have a 48% higher risk of high blood pressure and a 200% higher risk of heart attack compared to those who sleep 7–8 hours.
c_sleep_facts.detail: The heart and blood vessels need sleep for 'maintenance'. During deep sleep, blood pressure drops 10–20% (nocturnal dipping) — this is a critical 'rest period' for the cardiovascular system. People without nocturnal dipping (often due to poor sleep) have significantly higher cardiovascular risk.
details: Nocturnal dipping: blood pressure normally drops 10–20% during sleep — the heart and vessels get true rest.
Poor sleep eliminates nocturnal dipping — the heart works 24/7 with no rest, leading to cumulative damage.
CRP (C-reactive protein) — an inflammation marker — rises with poor sleep, an independent risk factor for atherosclerosis.
Poor sleep increases fibrinogen (clotting protein) — increasing the risk of blood clot formation.
Sleeping under 6 hours continuously for 2 weeks: cardiovascular risk equivalent to smoking a pack a day.
Improving sleep from 6 to 7 hours significantly reduced cardiovascular risk according to the 2019 NHANES study.

c_sleep_facts.label: Mood Stabilization
c_sleep_facts.desc: Adequate sleep helps control emotions better, reduces anxiety, irritability, and makes it easier to maintain training motivation.
c_sleep_facts.keyFact: Poor sleep makes the amygdala (emotional center) react 60% more strongly to negative stimuli — explaining why tired people are more easily irritated and have less emotional control.
c_sleep_facts.detail: REM sleep plays a particularly important role in emotional regulation. During REM, the brain reprocesses emotional memories in a low-noradrenaline environment — helping 'detoxify' negative emotions without causing additional stress. Matthew Walker calls this 'overnight therapy' — the natural nightly therapy.
details: The amygdala — the center of emotional processing and fear response — increases activity by 60% when sleep-deprived.
Connection between the prefrontal cortex (rational) and amygdala (emotional) weakens with poor sleep — loss of emotional control.
REM sleep 'detoxes' emotions: reprocesses memories in a low-stress environment, reducing the intensity of negative emotions.
Chronic poor sleep doubles the risk of depression and triples the risk of anxiety according to long-term longitudinal studies.
The dopamine pathway (reward system) is also affected — poor sleep reduces feelings of pleasure and training motivation.
7–9 hours of good sleep is the foundation of mental health — no intervention can replace it.

c_sleep_stages.label: N1 — Light Drowsiness
c_sleep_stages.desc: Transition from wakefulness to sleep. The body starts to relax, heart rate slows.
c_sleep_stages.keyFact: N1 accounts for only 5% of sleep and is extremely easy to disrupt — this is the stage where you 'jerk awake' (hypnic jerk) and can still hear surrounding sounds.
c_sleep_stages.detail: N1 is the gateway between wakefulness and sleep — the brain begins transitioning from beta waves (alert) to alpha then theta waves (drowsy). This is the shortest and most sensitive stage: even a small light or sound can fully awaken you.
details: Heart rate slows, muscles relax, body temperature begins to drop slightly.
Brain waves shift from alpha (8–12 Hz, relaxed) to theta (4–7 Hz, drowsy) — consciousness fades.
Hypnic jerk: the brain misinterprets sudden muscle relaxation as 'falling' and sends a contraction signal.
In N1, you can still hear sounds and see hazy images (hypnagogic hallucination).
If woken from N1, you often say 'I wasn't asleep' — even though you've been asleep for a few minutes.
N1 repeats shorter in later cycles — the body 'goes deeper' faster once used to sleeping.

c_sleep_stages.label: N2 — Light Sleep
c_sleep_stages.desc: Body temperature drops, heart rate slows further. Sleep spindles appear — important for memory.
c_sleep_stages.keyFact: N2 accounts for ~50% of total sleep — this is where 'sleep spindles' appear, helping transfer information from short-term to long-term memory and protecting sleep from disruption.
c_sleep_stages.detail: N2 is where sleep truly begins — consciousness is almost completely off, harder to wake than N1. Sleep spindles (bursts of high-frequency brain waves) appear in N2, playing a key role in consolidating procedural memory and motor skills. A 20-minute power nap contains enough N2 to improve afternoon performance.
details: Body temperature continues to drop, heart rate and breathing are slower and more regular than N1.
Sleep spindles: bursts of 12–15 Hz brain waves, lasting 0.5–3 seconds, appearing 1–2 times per minute in N2.
Sleep spindles inhibit sensory signals from the thalamus — 'soundproofing' the brain from external stimulation.
K-complexes: high-amplitude single brain waves, responding to sudden noise — protecting sleep from disruption.
N2 is critical for procedural memory — learning an instrument, sports technique, hand operations.
A 20-minute power nap is enough to enter N2 and benefit from sleep spindles — N3 is not needed for memory benefits.

c_sleep_stages.label: N3 — Deep Sleep
c_sleep_stages.desc: The most important stage for physical recovery. Growth hormone is released. Hardest to wake from.
c_sleep_stages.keyFact: N3 (slow-wave sleep) is the body's 'major overhaul' stage — GH is secreted at its peak, the immune system recovers, and the brain flushes harmful waste via the glymphatic system. Losing N3 = losing recovery.
c_sleep_stages.detail: N3 is the peak of sleep — hardest to wake from, and if woken abruptly causes 'sleep inertia' (grogginess, disorientation). The brain's glymphatic system is most active in N3, flushing out beta-amyloid and tau protein — substances linked to Alzheimer's. Chronic N3 deprivation is a risk factor for dementia.
details: Delta waves (0.5–4 Hz) dominate — the slowest and highest-amplitude brain waves in all of sleep.
Growth Hormone (GH) is secreted 70–80% in N3 — gym training without enough N3 is wasted effort.
The glymphatic system is most active: cerebrospinal fluid flushes metabolic waste, including beta-amyloid (Alzheimer-linked).
The immune system produces cytokines and increases T-cell activity — N3 deficiency reduces vaccine response and infection resistance.
N3 is most abundant in the first 3 hours of the night — sleeping late means losing most of N3 even if total sleep time is unchanged.
N3 cannot be 'made up' with a nap — sleeping early is needed for the circadian system to support N3 naturally.

points.label: GH secreted 70–80%
points.note: Recovery of muscles, bones, tendons — peak in N3

c_sleep_stages.label: REM — Dreaming
c_sleep_stages.desc: Brain is highly active. Consolidates emotional memory, processes complex information, and restores mental health.
c_sleep_stages.keyFact: During REM, the brain is almost as active as when awake — but muscles are temporarily 'paralyzed'. This is the stage for emotional processing, creativity, and the 'overnight therapy' Matthew Walker describes.
c_sleep_stages.detail: REM (Rapid Eye Movement) is the strangest stage of sleep: the brain is active like when awake, but the body is nearly motionless (muscle atonia — so you don't act out your dreams). This is when the brain integrates information, processes complex emotions, and creates creative connections.
details: Eyes move rapidly under the eyelids — the brain is 'reviewing' and processing daytime memories.
Muscle atonia (temporary paralysis) caused by brain suppressing the spinal cord — preventing the body from acting out dreams.
REM is most abundant in the early morning (4–6 AM) — waking early or setting an alarm cuts the most important REM.
Emotional processing in a low-noradrenaline environment — memories are 'replayed' without the accompanying stress response.
Creative problem-solving: many inventions and solutions appear after REM sleep — the brain makes non-linear connections.
REM deficiency is linked to PTSD (brain can't 'detox' traumatic memories), depression, and anxiety.

c_sleep_hygiene.label: Fixed sleep-wake window
c_sleep_hygiene.content: You don't need to be perfectly precise, but try to stay within 60 minutes across days including weekends. The body runs on a 24-hour biological rhythm (circadian rhythm). Consistent sleep times help the body predict and prepare melatonin production at the right moment.
c_sleep_hygiene.tip: Set an alarm to WAKE (not to sleep). Waking at the right time matters more than going to bed at the right time.
c_sleep_hygiene.keyFact: Keeping a consistent wake time (±30 minutes) 7 days a week is the single most powerful intervention to improve sleep quality — more important than even bedtime.
c_sleep_hygiene.detail: The biological clock (circadian clock) in the suprachiasmatic nucleus controls the entire sleep-wake cycle, hormones, body temperature, and hundreds of physiological processes. This 'clock' needs stable signals — and the most important signal is the morning wake-up time.
details: The body begins preparing for sleep 14–16 hours after waking — consistent wake time = consistent sleepiness time.
Weekend sleep extension of 2–3 extra hours causes 'social jetlag' — equivalent to flying across 2–3 time zones every week.
Keep variation within 60 minutes across days — the brain needs consistency to secrete melatonin at the right time.
Morning sunlight (5–10 minutes) is the strongest 'clock reset' — activates cortisol for alertness and stabilizes circadian rhythm.
Accumulated social jetlag: sleeping late and waking late on weekends then 'forcing' an early wake on Monday creates chronic fatigue.
Set a WAKE alarm because wake time is easier to control than sleep time — sleepiness appears naturally when the time is right.

points.note: Biological clock needs stable daily signals

c_sleep_hygiene.label: Reduce bright light in the evening
c_sleep_hygiene.content: Blue light from screens suppresses melatonin — the hormone signaling 'time to sleep'. Dim the lights, reduce screen brightness from 9–10 PM. Use Night Shift/Night Mode on devices.
c_sleep_hygiene.tip: Warm light (amber/yellow) at night suppresses melatonin less than white/blue light.
c_sleep_hygiene.keyFact: Just 10 minutes of 480nm blue light (phone screen) at 9 PM delays melatonin secretion by 90 minutes — you won't feel sleepy until 11 PM even though your body needs sleep from 9:30 PM.
c_sleep_hygiene.detail: Melanopsin cells in the retina (ipRGC) are particularly sensitive to 480nm light (blue) — this light sends a 'daytime' signal to the brain even with just a few minutes of exposure. The body cannot distinguish between sunlight and a phone screen at this wavelength.
details: Melanopsin in ipRGC is the 'special' light sensor — most sensitive to 480nm.
Blue light → 'daytime' signal → brain suppresses pineal gland → stops melatonin secretion.
Night Shift/Night Mode reduces blue light by 50–80% — effective but does not completely eliminate it.
Blue light blocking glasses are more effective than Night Mode because they block at the source.
Red/amber sleep lights (<590nm) have almost no effect on melatonin — ideal for bedrooms after 9 PM.
Bathroom lights are often very bright and white — switch to a small or warm bulb after 9 PM.

points.label: 10 min = 90 min delay
points.note: Phone at 9 PM → not sleepy until 11 PM

c_sleep_hygiene.label: Reduce stimulants before sleep
c_sleep_hygiene.content: Caffeine has a half-life of 5–6 hours — coffee at 3 PM still has ½ its amount in your blood at 9 PM. Avoid heavy exercise within 2 hours of bedtime. Avoid arguments, stressful work, and emotionally charged news.
c_sleep_hygiene.tip: Replace evening coffee with warm herbal tea (ginger, chamomile) if you need to drink something.
c_sleep_hygiene.keyFact: Caffeine consumed at 3 PM still has 50% left in your blood at 9 PM — and if you are caffeine-sensitive, ¼ is still there at 1 AM. You're not 'unaffected' — your brain just no longer recognizes the blocked adenosine.
c_sleep_hygiene.detail: Caffeine works by blocking adenosine receptors — the substance that accumulates while you're awake, creating sleepiness. Caffeine doesn't 'turn off' fatigue — it just hides the tired signal. Adenosine continues to accumulate and when caffeine wears off, the 'caffeine crash' hits hard.
details: Caffeine half-life 5–6 hours: 200mg at 3 PM → 100mg at 8–9 PM → 50mg at 1–2 AM.
Adenosine buildup still happens after caffeine — when caffeine wears off, adenosine floods back to the receptors → strong 'crash'.
Heavy exercise within 2 hours of sleep raises core body temperature and cortisol — delaying sleep by 1–2 hours.
Bad news, arguments, stressful work emails at night activate the amygdala — cortisol rises, hard to relax.
Alcohol speeds up falling asleep but destroys sleep architecture: suppresses REM and causes midnight awakenings.
Cutting caffeine after 2 PM and avoiding heavy exercise before 8 PM are the 2 simplest changes with the biggest impact.

c_sleep_hygiene.label: Optimize the bedroom
c_sleep_hygiene.content: Ideal sleep temperature: 18–21°C. The body needs temperature to drop to enter deep sleep. Dark room (blackout curtains or sleep mask), quiet (earplugs if needed). Bed is only for sleeping — no working, no watching movies in bed.
c_sleep_hygiene.tip: Bed = sleep signal. Working in bed makes the brain associate bed with an alert state.
c_sleep_hygiene.keyFact: Room temperature 18–21°C helps core body temperature drop 1–2°C — a necessary condition to enter N3 deep sleep. Too hot or too cold both significantly reduce N3.
c_sleep_hygiene.detail: An ideal bedroom follows 3 principles: dark, cool, and quiet. Most important is 'stimulus control' — associating bed with only one behavior: sleep. The brain learns by Pavlovian association — if you work or watch movies in bed, the brain associates 'bed = alert state'.
details: 18–21°C is the 'golden threshold': core body temperature needs to drop 1–2°C for the brain to activate N3.
Completely dark room: even a small night light is enough for melanopsin to detect and slightly delay melatonin.
Irregular noise (traffic, neighbors) causes micro-arousals (brief unrecognized awakenings) — disrupting sleep architecture.
White noise or pink noise helps mask random noise — the brain doesn't react to consistent sound.
Stimulus control: bed is only for sleeping and intimacy — no phone, no laptop, no TV.
Blackout curtains are the best bedroom investment — especially if you sleep late and need to block early morning light.

c_sleep_trouble.title: In bed but can't fall asleep
tips: Don't keep watching the clock
Don't force sleep — relax your body instead of forcing your eyes shut
Slow diaphragmatic breathing for 3–5 minutes
Read a paper book lightly, no screens
If lying more than 30 minutes without sleeping: get up gently for 10 minutes then try again

c_sleep_trouble.title: Sleeping late due to work
tips: Set a 'close the day' time — after that, no new work accepted
Write down 3 unfinished tasks to clear your mind
Switch to a short 10-minute evening routine
Don't work in bed
Computer screen: use Night Shift/Night Mode from 9 PM

c_sleep_trouble.title: Very sleepy in the evening but wide awake in bed
tips: Common cause: screen use too close to bedtime
Room lighting still too bright
Overthinking tomorrow's tasks
Late caffeine or too little movement during the day
Fix: increase morning light + increase daily walking + evening journaling

c_sleep_7day.label: Record honestly, don't force
c_sleep_7day.action: Record your actual sleep times — don't try to sleep earlier right away
c_sleep_7day.keyFact: Knowing your actual baseline matters more than immediately changing it — you can't adjust what you haven't measured.
c_sleep_7day.detail: Day 1 is an observation day, no intervention. Honest records of actual sleep time (not the time you want to sleep) let you see the real gap to close — and avoid changes so drastic they backfire.
details: Record 3 data points: time into bed, time actually asleep, time woke up — not your desired times.
Also note: feeling upon waking (refreshed/tired), estimated total sleep time, and special factors (stress, late movie...).
Don't try to sleep earlier today — abrupt changes leave you lying awake, creating sleep anxiety.
Use a phone note or small bedside notebook — record immediately upon waking while memory is fresh.
After 7 days, a pattern will emerge: which day do you typically sleep latest? Fri/Sat or weekdays? Why?
This data is the 'map' for the next 6 days to have a specific direction instead of blind changes.

c_sleep_7day.label: Screens off earlier
c_sleep_7day.action: Turn off screens 15 minutes earlier than usual
c_sleep_7day.keyFact: Just 15 minutes without a screen before sleep creates a melatonin window large enough for the body to start 'receiving the sleep signal' — the smallest step with the biggest impact.
c_sleep_7day.detail: Instead of demanding 'no screens for 2 hours' — something almost no one maintains — just push back 15 minutes from yesterday's habit. The goal is building a lasting habit, not a perfect one-night change.
details: If you turned off screens at 11:30 PM yesterday, turn them off at 11:15 PM today — just 15 minutes, no more.
Replace screen time with a paper book, a gentle podcast, or 15 minutes of hand journaling.
Night Mode / Night Shift still helps but doesn't replace turning off screens — the brain is still stimulated by content.
Phone notifications after 9–10 PM are the biggest source of disruption — enable Do Not Disturb before bed.
Charging your phone outside the bedroom removes the temptation to 'just check one more thing' — use a regular alarm clock.
After a few days of 15 minutes, your body will start getting sleepy earlier naturally — continue pushing back on Day 4.

c_sleep_7day.label: Morning sunlight
c_sleep_7day.action: Go outside or open curtains for 5 minutes after waking
c_sleep_7day.keyFact: Morning sunlight in the first 5–10 minutes after waking is the strongest circadian signal — 'resetting the biological clock' and pulling evening sleepiness earlier.
c_sleep_7day.detail: Daytime light (especially 480nm blue from the sky) turns off melatonin and triggers morning cortisol — setting the body's 24-hour clock. No intervention is as simple yet effective as 5 minutes of morning sun for pulling bedtime earlier.
details: Outdoor sunlight (even on cloudy days) contains 10,000–100,000 lux — indoor lighting is only 300–500 lux, not enough to reset circadian rhythm.
Intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGC) receive 480nm light → signal to the suprachiasmatic nucleus → cortisol rises → natural alertness.
Every hour of daytime light you receive in the morning = pulls evening sleepiness about 15 minutes earlier.
No direct sunlight needed — sitting by an open window, standing on a balcony, or walking outside all work equally.
Combine with a short 5-minute outdoor walk to raise morning body temperature — increases alertness and circadian stability.
Strong morning light also improves mood (serotonin) and reduces SAD (Seasonal Affective Disorder) symptoms.

c_sleep_7day.detail: Day 4 is the first real 'pull' of bedtime earlier. After 3 days of circadian preparation, the body has enough 'sleep pressure' built up early enough that going to bed 15 minutes sooner doesn't cause insomnia.
details: Get into bed 15 minutes earlier than the average time recorded on Day 1 — not the time you 'want' to sleep.
If not feeling sleepy after 20–30 minutes: don't force it — read or breathe slowly instead of watching the clock.
Combine with a small pre-sleep ritual: brush teeth, turn off lights, 3 minutes of diaphragmatic breathing — signaling the brain 'time to sleep'.
Sleep pressure (adenosine buildup) is strong enough after 16–17 hours awake — if waking on time (Days 1–3), sleep pressure arrives on schedule.
No naps longer than 30 minutes today — long naps reduce evening sleep pressure, making it harder to sleep earlier.
Accept that the first night might take 20–30 minutes longer than usual — this is normal when starting to change.

c_sleep_7day.label: Cut late caffeine
c_sleep_7day.keyFact: Cutting caffeine after 2 PM is the single change with the biggest impact on N3 (deep sleep) quality — even if you 'feel unaffected by caffeine'.
c_sleep_7day.detail: Many people believe they are caffeine-insensitive — but EEG research shows afternoon caffeine still significantly reduces N3 (slow-wave sleep) even when the person says they 'sleep normally'. Deep sleep quality is affected without you realizing it.
details: Caffeine half-life 5–7 hours (depending on CYP1A2 gene) — slow metabolizers: 3 PM coffee is still 50% at midnight.
Even people who are 'caffeine-insensitive' still experience reduced N3 when caffeine is in the blood — they just don't notice the difficulty sleeping.
Reduced N3 = reduced GH secretion, reduced muscle recovery, reduced immunity — even if total sleep time is unchanged.
Hidden caffeine sources: green tea (~50mg/cup), Coca-Cola (~35mg/can), dark chocolate (~20mg/piece), caffeine-containing headache medicine.
Replace afternoon coffee with herbal tea (chamomile, ginger, lavender) or warm lemon water — still a drinking ritual without caffeine.
After 1 week of cutting caffeine after 2 PM, most people report sleeping deeper and feeling more alert in the morning.

c_sleep_7day.label: Add an evening routine
c_sleep_7day.action: Add 10 minutes: light stretching + slow breathing before bed
c_sleep_7day.keyFact: A 10-minute evening routine creates a 'bridge' between the active state and sleep — the brain learns by association: a repeated chain of actions = signal 'time to sleep'.
c_sleep_7day.detail: A pre-sleep routine is Pavlovian conditioning applied to sleep. After a few weeks of repetition, just starting the chain of actions (brush teeth → turn off lights → stretch → slow breathing) and the brain automatically shifts to 'sleep-ready' mode. No need for a long routine — 10 minutes creates a strong enough signal.
details: 10-minute structure: 3 minutes light stretching (neck, shoulders, back) → 3 minutes diaphragmatic breathing → 4 minutes reading a paper book or journaling.
Consistency matters more than perfection — 10 minutes every night is better than 45 minutes 3 times a week.
Don't check email or work messages during these 10 minutes — this is the official 'close the day' time.
Write down 3 things accomplished today and 3 things for tomorrow — 'unload' the mind, reduce repetitive thoughts when lying down.
Room temperature: start lowering the AC or opening a window slightly during the evening routine — signaling the body to prepare for deep sleep.
After 7–14 days of repetition, you'll start feeling sleepy when you begin the routine — the brain has learned the association.

c_sleep_7day.label: Keep wake time stable
c_sleep_7day.action: Wake at the right time, no more than 1 extra hour of weekend sleep
c_sleep_7day.keyFact: Weekend sleep extension of 2+ hours causes 'social jetlag' — resetting all 6 days of circadian improvement. A consistent wake time ±30 minutes is the one thing you can't skip.
c_sleep_7day.detail: Day 7 is not the finish line — it's the foundation for the next week. A consistent wake time 7 days a week (including weekends) is the only intervention proven to maintain long-term circadian improvement. All 6 previous days point toward this goal.
details: Social jetlag: sleeping late and waking late on weekends is equivalent to flying across 2–3 time zones — and it repeats every week.
Waking 1 hour later on weekends is the safe limit — 2+ hours starts affecting circadian rhythm.
If sleep-deprived: go to bed earlier on Friday/Saturday night instead of waking later Saturday/Sunday morning — protect wake time.
After these 7 days, you have: clear baseline, reduced evening light, morning light exposure, earlier bedtime, no late caffeine, and an evening routine.
Next week: continue pulling bedtime back 15 minutes every 2–3 days until you reach your target bedtime.
Key point: no need for perfection — 'good enough' sleep 6/7 nights a week is better than 'perfect' sleep 2 nights.

c_sleep_routine_r60.action: Stop heavy work, finalize tomorrow's tasks
c_sleep_routine_r60.keyFact: The decision to stop working at minute 60 — not 'when I finish' — is the most important step of any routine. The brain needs 45–60 minutes to shift from 'work mode' to 'sleep mode'.
c_sleep_routine_r60.detail: 'I'll stop when I'm done' is the biggest trap. Work is never truly finished — there's always another email, another task. Set a hard 'end of day' time like an unbreakable appointment, not a vague goal.
details: The brain needs a 45–60 minute wind-down to reduce cortisol and shift from beta waves (focused) to alpha waves (relaxed) before deep sleep can occur.
Stopping heavy work doesn't mean stopping completely — but don't start new tasks, open emails, or join meetings after this point.
Finalize tomorrow's work by writing your 1–3 most important morning tasks — your brain can 'let go' of them instead of processing them overnight.
The 'concern dump' technique: write down everything you're worried about — the brain stops replaying them once they're clearly recorded.
System notifications (Slack, email, phone): enable 'Do Not Disturb' right now — not 10 minutes later.
Consistency in your daily end time matters more than any technical measure — the body starts preparing for sleep from a fixed time signal.

c_sleep_routine_r60.action: Final phone check, then put it away
c_sleep_routine_r60.keyFact: The 'last check' is the most important moment — after it the phone must leave arm's reach. Charging your phone outside the bedroom is the simplest physical change to break the 'just one more scroll' cycle.
c_sleep_routine_r60.detail: A phone in the bedroom — even with the screen off — creates constant psychological pull. Research shows the mere presence of a phone (even face-down) still reduces relaxation and slows the transition to rest.
details: Intentional check: open, read, reply if needed, then put it down — don't scroll aimlessly after checking.
Don't reply to work emails or messages after this point — replying creates an expectation of '24/7 availability' that is hard to break later.
Phone outside the bedroom: use a regular alarm clock instead — completely eliminating the 'need it for the alarm' excuse.
If you must keep the phone in the room: face it down, silence all notifications, and place it out of reach from the bed.
Blue light from phone screens (480nm) suppresses melatonin even after less than 10 minutes — minute 50 is the latest you should cut off.
Replace with: gentle podcasts (no news), ambient music, or simply silence — the brain needs less stimulation, not more.

c_sleep_routine_r60.action: Dim room lights, switch on warm night light
c_sleep_routine_r60.keyFact: Reducing light intensity below 50 lux (equivalent to candlelight) for 45 minutes before sleep lets the pineal gland start releasing melatonin — the body can't distinguish 'white LED' from 'daytime'.
c_sleep_routine_r60.detail: The human light system evolved without electricity. At dusk, light shifts from blue (daytime) to red/orange (sunset) — the signal telling the body 'it's getting dark'. Modern room lighting (especially white LEDs) completely disrupts this biological signal.
details: Melanopsin in the retina is most sensitive to 480nm light (blue) — exactly the dominant wavelength in white LEDs and modern screens.
The body needs light to drop below 50 lux (candlelight) for at least 30 minutes before bed for the pineal gland to start releasing adequate melatonin.
Warm night lights (2700K–3000K, orange/yellow) contain far less 480nm light than daytime white bulbs (5000–6500K) — the most practical replacement.
Red light (<590nm) barely stimulates melanopsin — ideal for the bedroom after 9 PM if you need light to move around.
Bathrooms often have very white, bright lights — replace with a small warm bulb or night light when using the bathroom after 9 PM.
Smart bulbs can be scheduled to automatically dim to 2700K at 9 PM — one-time investment, applied every night without effort.

c_sleep_routine_r60.action: Warm shower or wash face, personal hygiene
c_sleep_routine_r60.keyFact: A warm shower at 40–42°C for 10 minutes, 40–60 minutes before sleep, helps your core body temperature drop quickly afterward — significantly accelerating entry into deep N3 sleep.
c_sleep_routine_r60.detail: The thermal paradox: a hot shower actually helps you sleep cooler. Warm water dilates peripheral blood vessels → heat radiates out through skin → core body temperature drops after you step out. The brain reads 'core temperature dropping' = 'time for deep sleep'. No bathtub? A 15-minute foot soak works nearly as well.
details: Core body temperature must drop 1–2°C to enter N3 (deep sleep) — a warm shower accelerates this through the skin heat-dissipation mechanism.
Ideal water temperature: 40–42°C — warm enough to dilate blood vessels without prolonged discomfort.
Optimal timing: 10–15 minute shower, 40–60 minutes before sleep — giving core temperature time to drop to the optimal level.
Warm foot soak for 15 minutes: feet have high blood vessel density — nearly as effective as a full body shower, easier to do.
Avoid showering too hot (>43°C) right before bed: the body needs extra time to cool down, potentially delaying rather than improving sleep.
Combine with warm lighting in the bathroom — don't turn on bright white lights when showering to avoid disrupting the melatonin signal forming.

c_sleep_routine_r60.action: Light stretching: neck, shoulders, back, hips (5–10 min)
c_sleep_routine_r60.keyFact: Light stretching for 5–10 minutes before sleep reduces cortisol, releases tension accumulated in muscles after a long day, and sends a 'safety' signal to the nervous system — allowing the body to shift into recovery mode.
c_sleep_routine_r60.detail: Tight muscles (especially neck, shoulders, back) signal that the sympathetic nervous system is still activated. Stretching doesn't just relax muscles — it activates the parasympathetic nervous system through the muscle-brain reflex, slowing heart rate and preparing the body for sleep.
details: The neck, shoulder, and upper back region accumulates the most tension — sitting at a computer all day creates chronic tightness that needs releasing before sleep.
Stretching activates muscle receptors (Golgi tendon organs) → 'safety' signals sent to brain → sympathetic nervous system naturally reduces activity.
Don't push hard: the goal is relaxation, not a workout. Hold each position for 30–60 seconds, breathe slowly — don't stretch to the point of pain.
5 basics: chin tuck (neck), shoulder roll (shoulders), thoracic twist (upper back), child pose (lower back), legs up the wall (legs/hips).
Combine slow breathing while stretching — exhale longer than inhale (4 sec in / 6–8 sec out) noticeably increases relaxation effectiveness.
Especially effective for heavy exercisers — helps post-exercise cortisol drop faster and muscles recover better during N3 sleep.

c_sleep_routine_r60.action: Read a paper book or listen to gentle music
c_sleep_routine_r60.keyFact: Reading a paper book for 20 minutes before sleep reduces stress by 68% (University of Sussex 2009) — more effective than listening to music (61%), drinking tea (54%), or taking a walk (42%). The brain 'escapes' real problems by immersing in a story.
c_sleep_routine_r60.detail: Paper books are perfect for this moment for 3 reasons: no blue light, no notifications, and linear content (not infinite scrolling). The brain is gently stimulated by a story rather than being pulled tight by real-world information.
details: University of Sussex (2009): just 6 minutes of reading lowers heart rate, muscle tension, and stress levels by 68% — faster than any other relaxation method tested.
Paper book vs. e-reader: paper has no self-emitted light, no notifications, no 'next content' suggestions — far less stimulating to the brain.
Ideal content: light fiction, interesting but non-stressful non-fiction — avoid professional books, news, or cognitively demanding content.
Soft music (60–80 BPM, no lyrics or gentle lyrics) synchronizes heart rate with musical tempo — naturally reducing heart rate through entrainment.
Gentle podcasts are a good option if you don't want to read — avoid professional podcasts, news, or controversial content.
Don't read on phone/tablet — even with night mode, the brain still reflexively 'scrolls', 'swipes', 'checks' from established habits.

c_sleep_routine_r60.keyFact: Exhaling longer than inhaling (1:2 ratio, e.g., inhale 4 sec — exhale 8 sec) activates the vagus nerve and lowers heart rate within 60–90 seconds — the only method that can directly intervene in the autonomic nervous system by will.
c_sleep_routine_r60.detail: Breathing is the only bridge between the autonomic nervous system (normally operating outside conscious control) and consciousness. When exhaling slowly and deeply, the vagus nerve is activated → heart rate slows → blood pressure drops → cortisol falls → body shifts into recovery mode.
details: The parasympathetic nervous system is activated mainly through exhalation — inhalation mildly activates sympathetic, exhalation strongly activates parasympathetic.
Optimal pre-sleep breathing ratio: inhale 4 sec → hold 4 sec (optional) → exhale 6–8 sec — exhale at least twice as long as inhale.
Diaphragmatic breathing (belly expands on inhale, not chest) maximizes volume per breath → fewer breaths → naturally slower heart rate.
4-7-8 method (inhale 4, hold 7, exhale 8): effective quickly but difficult for beginners — start with 4-0-6 which is simpler.
Box breathing (4-4-4-4): good for daytime and stress relief — but 4-6-8 is better before sleep because the exhale is noticeably longer.
Just 3–5 minutes is enough for the parasympathetic nervous system to gain dominance — the shortest of all evidence-based relaxation techniques.

A consistent wake time (unchanged even after a late night) matters more than bedtime — accumulated sleep pressure will naturally pull bedtime earlier.
First night sleeping 15 min earlier: if not asleep after 20 minutes, quietly get up, read lightly for 10 minutes then try again — don't force it.

Better replacement: paper books (warm lamp, no screen, linear content with no 'next episode'). Gentle podcasts are also acceptable.

c_sleep_routine_mistakes.detail: Social jetlag is the phenomenon where weekend sleep/wake times diverge significantly from weekday times — causing all the symptoms of real jet lag: fatigue, poor focus, difficulty sleeping at the usual time Sunday night. This is a self-sustaining cycle: sleep in → stay up late → can't sleep Sunday → sleep-deprived Monday → sleep in again.
details: Social jetlag: mismatch between the biological clock (circadian) and social clock — staying up late on weekends = flying to a different time zone each week.
Munich Chronotype Study: social jetlag of 2+ hours is associated with 33% higher risk of obesity, cardiovascular disease, and depression.
Sleeping in doesn't 'pay back sleep debt' — sleeping deficient Monday through Friday, catching up Saturday doesn't restore the accumulated cognitive damage.

If sleep-deprived on weekends: go to bed earlier Friday/Saturday night instead of waking up later Saturday/Sunday morning — protect your wake time.
Long-term solution: improve sleep quality during the week (not weekend catchup hours) — sleeping deeper in 7 hours beats sleeping 9 hours of shallow sleep.

c_sleep_routine_mistakes.label: Drinking alcohol to fall asleep
c_sleep_routine_mistakes.right: Alcohol helps you fall asleep but destroys deep sleep and REM
c_sleep_routine_mistakes.keyFact: Alcohol is a central nervous system depressant — it helps you fall asleep faster but suppresses REM and causes mid-night waking as the liver metabolizes it. Post-alcohol sleep is 'sedation' not 'restorative sleep'.
c_sleep_routine_mistakes.detail: Alcohol reduces sleep onset latency — this is why many people use it to sleep. Result: enough hours of sleep but terrible sleep quality.
details: Alcohol helps you fall asleep faster by increasing GABA (inhibitory) and reducing glutamate (excitatory) — effective for the first 1–2 hours.
After 4–5 hours, the liver converts alcohol to acetaldehyde — this substance stimulates the nervous system, creating 'rebound arousal' and mid-night waking.
REM is clearly suppressed: studies show alcohol reduces REM by 20–40% in the first half of the night — losing exactly the most important psychological and emotional recovery stage.
Alcohol causes dehydration and increased nighttime urination — additional sources of mid-night waking beyond rebound arousal.
Snoring and sleep apnea worsen significantly after drinking alcohol — throat muscles relax more than usual.
Replacement: if you need evening relaxation, warm herbal tea (chamomile, lavender, ginger), a warm shower, or slow breathing — no side effects.

A gentle routine (stretching, slow breathing, reading) activates the parasympathetic system — naturally lowering cortisol and opening the 'door' for melatonin to rise.

Melatonin and cortisol have an inverse relationship — when one rises, the other falls. High evening cortisol = suppresses melatonin secretion from the pineal gland.
'Trying to sleep' creates sleep anxiety → activates more cortisol → harder to sleep — this is the spiral that many insomniacs are trapped in.
Slow breathing (inhale 4 sec, exhale 6–8 sec) activates the vagus nerve → lowers heart rate → reduces cortisol within 3–5 minutes.
Light stretching (not heavy exercise) lowers cortisol faster than sitting still — relaxed muscles send 'safety' signals to the brain.
Cortisol naturally reaches its lowest around midnight–2 AM — a routine helps accelerate this drop so you can sleep earlier instead of waiting for it.
